countries.name: Portugal
countries.tagline: A narrow Atlantic country with some 250 native grapes, two of the world's great fortified wines and a table-wine revolution still gathering speed.

stats.note: OIV, State of the World Wine Sector in 2025 (May 2026): vineyard 171 kha (10th in the world), production 6.0 mhl (-14% on 2024, lowest since 2011), consumption a record 5.6 mhl, exports 3.4 mhl worth about 1.0 bn EUR. IVV put the 2025/26 campaign at 5.9 mhl.

countries.overview:
Portugal is small on the map and enormous in the glass. From the granite hills of the Minho to the cork-oak plains of the Alentejo it covers barely 560 km north to south, yet it holds about 171,000 hectares of vines (the world's tenth-largest vineyard in 2025) and a grape list that runs to roughly 250 native varieties. Almost none of them were planted elsewhere until recently. Touriga Nacional, Touriga Franca, Baga, Alvarinho, Arinto, Encruzado: these are names you learn in Portugal because this is where they live.

The country's fame was built on two fortified wines made for export. Port, from the schist terraces of the Douro, was shaped by English merchants who needed a wine that survived the sea and suited a cold northern climate; the Douro became one of the world's first legally delimited wine regions in 1756, a century before Bordeaux had its classification. Madeira, from an island 1,000 km out in the Atlantic, was cooked by tropical voyages until merchants learned to recreate the heat in warm lofts and stoves; it filled the glasses that toasted American independence. Behind them come two lesser-known sweet wines with long pedigrees: Moscatel de Setúbal, perfumed and amber, and Carcavelos, an almost-vanished fortified wine from the Lisbon coast now being nursed back to life.

For most of the 20th century the rest of Portugal's wine was made by cooperatives for a closed home market and the colonies, or blended into the sweet, slightly fizzy rosés (Mateus, Lancers) that conquered the post-war world. Joining the European Community in 1986 changed everything. Money, stainless steel, temperature control and young winemakers trained in Bordeaux, Montpellier and Davis arrived together. In the Douro, families who had sold grapes to Port shippers for generations started bottling dry reds under their own names; the group of five estates that marketed themselves as the Douro Boys in the early 2000s became the symbol of that change. The Alentejo grew from a cereal belt into the country's most popular wine region; the Dão rediscovered the finesse of its granite; Bairrada's growers rehabilitated the fearsome Baga grape.

The result is a wine culture that feels both very old and very young. Talha wine is still fermented in clay jars in the Alentejo much as the Romans did it; the ungrafted Ramisco vines of Colares grow in Atlantic dune sand that phylloxera never crossed; Pico Island's black-basalt vineyard walls are a UNESCO World Heritage landscape. At the same time a new generation is making low-intervention whites from Vinho Verde's mountain valleys, high-altitude reds from the Serra da Estrela and old-vine field blends from forgotten Douro hillsides.

Portugal also drinks its own wine with conviction. The OIV recorded a record 5.6 million hectolitres of domestic consumption in 2025, one of the highest per-head levels in the world, even as production fell to 6.0 mhl after a season of record rain followed by heat and disease. Exports are worth about 1 billion euros a year; Port alone is close to a third of that value. The sector's live issue in 2026 is oversupply: the Douro has more vineyard than the shrinking Port market can absorb, and the annual Port quota (the beneficio) fell from 104,000 pipes in 2023 to 75,000 in 2025 before edging up to 76,000 for the 2026 harvest.

history.title: Rome reaches Lusitania
history.text: Vines were probably first planted by Tartessians and Phoenicians in the south, but it was Rome that spread viticulture after conquering the province it called Lusitania. Roman wine presses and dolia have been excavated across the Alentejo, and the clay-jar (talha) tradition of the Vidigueira area is the living descendant of that technology.

history.title: Treaty of Windsor
history.text: England and Portugal signed the alliance that is still in force today, the oldest diplomatic alliance in the world. It gave English merchants privileges in Portuguese ports, and trade in wine, cloth and salt cod grew under its protection. Viana do Castelo and Monção shipped red 'Viana' wine to England long before Port existed.

history.title: Brandy meets Douro wine
history.text: The best-known Port origin story has two Liverpool wine merchants finding the abbot of Lamego adding brandy to his wine during fermentation. True or not, the late 17th century is when English shippers in Porto began fortifying Douro red to stabilise it for the sea voyage, creating the sweet, strong style that became Port.

history.title: Methuen Treaty
history.text: John Methuen's commercial treaty set duties on Portuguese wine in England at a third below those on French wine, in exchange for Portugal opening its market to English woollens. With England at war with France, Port became the patriotic drink of Georgian England and the Douro's fortunes were made.

history.title: Pombal demarcates the Douro
history.text: After a price collapse blamed on adulteration and the power of the English shippers, the Marquis of Pombal created the Companhia Geral da Agricultura das Vinhas do Alto Douro by royal charter of 10 September 1756. It drew a legal boundary around the Douro vineyards, graded them, and between 1758 and 1761 set 335 granite boundary stones (the marcos pombalinos) around the best land. It is one of the first legally delimited and regulated wine regions in the world.

history.title: The Factory House
history.text: The British merchants of Porto, organised as a 'factory' (trading association), completed their club house on Rua do Infante Dom Henrique around 1790. It still hosts the weekly lunch of the Port shippers' association, where decanters of Vintage Port are passed to the left.

history.title: Forrester maps the river
history.text: Joseph James Forrester, an English merchant later made a baron, published his great map of the Douro in 1843 (with later editions) and campaigned against the over-fortification of Port. He drowned in 1861 when his boat overturned at the Cachão da Valeira rapids; legend says Dona Antónia Ferreira, aboard the same boat, was saved by her crinoline.

history.title: Oidium
history.text: Powdery mildew arrived from America in the early 1850s and devastated both Madeira and the Douro. On Madeira, many growers switched to sugar cane or replanted with hybrids; the noble Madeira varieties never fully recovered their pre-oidium area.

history.title: Phylloxera
history.text: The vine louse was identified in the Douro in the 1860s and wiped out much of the old vineyard by the 1880s. The ruins of abandoned terraces, the mortórios, still scar the hillsides. Replanting on American rootstocks pushed vineyards upriver into the Douro Superior, and a few ungrafted survivors, such as Quinta do Noval's Nacional parcel and the sand vineyards of Colares, became legends.

history.title: A map of demarcated regions
history.text: A burst of laws between 1907 and 1911, under the last kings and the first Republic, created or re-confirmed demarcated regions for Port and the Douro, Madeira, Moscatel de Setúbal, Carcavelos, Colares, Bucelas, Dão and Vinho Verde, laying the skeleton of the modern appellation system.

history.title: Estado Novo corporatism
history.text: Salazar's regime created the Instituto do Vinho do Porto (1933) and the Casa do Douro (1932) and pushed growers into cooperatives (the adegas cooperativas) from the 1940s onwards. The system guaranteed outlets but rewarded volume, and most Portuguese table wine was anonymous until the 1980s.

history.title: Mateus Rosé
history.text: Fernando van Zeller Guedes created a lightly sparkling, off-dry rosé for the export market and named it after the baroque Mateus Palace near Vila Real, whose image went on the flask-shaped bottle. Mateus and its rival Lancers (from José Maria da Fonseca) became among the best-selling wines in the world in the 1960s and 1970s; Mateus founded the fortune of Sogrape.

history.title: EU accession
history.text: Portugal joined the European Community on 1 January 1986. The Port shippers lost their export monopoly through Vila Nova de Gaia, so Douro estates could ship Port directly; EU funds paid for new wineries and the replanting of whole regions; and the DOC system was rebuilt on European lines.

history.title: UNESCO and the Douro Boys
history.text: The Alto Douro Wine Region was inscribed as a World Heritage cultural landscape in 2001 (24,600 ha core zone). In the same years Quinta do Crasto, Quinta do Vale Meão, Quinta do Vallado, Niepoort and Quinta Vale Dona Maria began promoting their dry Douro reds together as the Douro Boys, announcing the region's second life as a table-wine region.

history.title: Pico's lava vineyards listed
history.text: UNESCO inscribed the Landscape of the Pico Island Vineyard Culture, a grid of small walled plots (currais) built from black basalt to protect vines from wind and salt spray.

history.title: The Douro surplus
history.text: Falling Port sales forced the IVDP to cut the annual Port quota from 104,000 pipes (2023) to 90,000 (2024) and 75,000 (2025); it was set at 76,000 for 2026. Crisis distillation and calls to reform the beneficio system dominate the region's politics.

countries.classification:
Portugal uses the EU two-tier system with its own labels. The top tier is the DOP (Denominação de Origem Protegida), still almost universally written DOC (Denominação de Origem Controlada) on labels and by wine people; there are 30 wine DOPs registered with the EU (31 if you count Porto and Douro, which share one territory, as two, which the register does). The second tier is the IGP (Indicação Geográfica Protegida), labelled Vinho Regional: Minho, Transmontano, Duriense, Terras de Cister, Terras do Dão, Terras da Beira, Beira Atlântico, Lisboa, Tejo, Península de Setúbal, Alentejano, Algarve, Açores and Terras Madeirenses. Many of Portugal's most ambitious wines are Vinho Regional because the producer wanted to use grapes or blends outside the DOC rules. Below that is plain Vinho (wine without geographical indication).

Each region is policed by a Comissão Vitivinícola Regional (CVR), except the Douro (IVDP) and Madeira (IVBAM), where state institutes control both production and the fortified-wine trade. National policy is set by the Instituto da Vinha e do Vinho (IVV).

Label terms that matter: Reserva (higher quality, at least 0.5% above the minimum alcohol for the DOC); Grande Reserva; Garrafeira (for red, at least 30 months ageing including 12 in bottle; for white 12 months including 6 in bottle); Colheita (vintage); Quinta (single estate); Herdade (estate, used in the south); Escolha (selection). Port and Madeira have their own category systems, explained in their entries. Some DOCs contain subregions that may be named on the label (Vinho Verde has nine, Alentejo eight, Dão seven, Beira Interior three, Trás-os-Montes three).

Two quirks: the territory of the Douro carries two DOPs on one map, Porto for fortified wine and Douro for unfortified wines, and growers there need a quota (beneficio) to turn their grapes into Port; and on Madeira the DOP Madeira covers the fortified wine while Madeirense covers the island's young dry table wines.
countries.climate_soils:
Portugal is an Atlantic country with a Mediterranean south. The north-west (Minho, coastal Beiras) is green and wet, with 1,200 to 2,000 mm of rain a year falling on granite: perfect for fresh, acidic whites like Alvarinho and Loureiro. A chain of mountains (Peneda-Gerês, Marão, Alvão, Montemuro, Caramulo, Serra da Estrela) blocks the Atlantic rain from the interior, so the Douro, Trás-os-Montes and Beira Interior are progressively drier and more continental: the Douro Superior can see 400 mm of rain and summer days over 40 °C.

Geology splits the country too. The Douro is schist, a flaky rock that the vines' roots can penetrate and that stores what little water falls; this is why Port can only come from the schist core of the valley. The Dão and much of the Minho sit on granite, giving lean, perfumed wines. Bairrada has clay-limestone (the name comes from barro, clay), the key to Baga's tannic power and long life. Lisbon's coast mixes limestone, clay and, at Colares, pure Atlantic sand; Setúbal has limestone on the Arrábida hills and sand on the plain; the Alentejo is a mosaic of schist, granite, marble (around Estremoz and Borba) and red Mediterranean clays under hot, dry summers. The islands are volcanic: basalt and tuff on Madeira and the Azores, where wind, salt spray and humidity shape everything from vine training to the final wine.

grapes.name: Touriga Nacional
grapes.note: The flagship red. Native to the Dão, it gives small berries, deep colour, violet and bergamot perfume and firm tannin. Once scarce because of low yields, it was rescued by clonal selection in the 1970s and 1980s and is now planted everywhere, from Port to Alentejo.

grapes.name: Touriga Franca
grapes.note: The most planted grape in the Douro and the backbone of most Port blends: floral, dense, reliable and better than Nacional at handling heat. Also called Touriga Francesa.

grapes.name: Tinta Roriz
grapes.note: Tempranillo, known as Aragonez in the south. Widely planted across Douro, Dão and Alentejo; gives body and red fruit, but can be dilute when overcropped.

grapes.name: Baga
grapes.note: Bairrada's thick-skinned, late-ripening, high-acid, very tannic red. Notoriously difficult, it makes long-lived reds and some of Portugal's best traditional-method sparkling wines.

grapes.name: Castelão
grapes.note: Once the most planted red in Portugal (also called Periquita), the grape of the Setúbal Peninsula sands, where it gives supple, red-fruited wine.

grapes.name: Alicante Bouschet
grapes.note: A French teinturier (red-fleshed) that found its true home in the Alentejo, where Herdade do Mouchão has grown it since the early 20th century.

grapes.name: Trincadeira
grapes.note: Tinta Amarela in the Douro. Spicy and aromatic but rot-prone; a key Alentejo blending grape in hot, dry sites.

grapes.name: Alfrocheiro
grapes.note: A Dão native with bright acidity and red-berry fruit, increasingly bottled alone.

grapes.name: Ramisco
grapes.note: The rare, ungrafted, very tannic red of the Colares sand vineyards.

grapes.name: Tinta Negra
grapes.note: Madeira's workhorse, most of the island's grapes; since 2015 it may be named on labels.

grapes.name: Alvarinho
grapes.note: Albariño, the most prestigious grape of Vinho Verde, historically concentrated in Monção e Melgaço. Peach, citrus and minerality, with ageing potential.

grapes.name: Loureiro
grapes.note: Floral, laurel-scented Vinho Verde grape of the Lima and Cávado valleys.

grapes.name: Arinto
grapes.note: Pedernã in Vinho Verde. Bracing natural acidity that survives heat, which makes it valuable from Bucelas to the Alentejo.

grapes.name: Encruzado
grapes.note: The Dão's great white: textured, ageworthy, able to take oak like a fine white Burgundy.

grapes.name: Fernão Pires
grapes.note: Maria Gomes in Bairrada. The most planted white in Portugal, aromatic and versatile, central to Tejo and Bairrada wines and sparkling bases.

grapes.name: Antão Vaz
grapes.note: The Alentejo's best white, from Vidigueira: full-bodied with tropical fruit.

grapes.name: Moscatel Graúdo and Moscatel Roxo
grapes.note: Muscat of Alexandria and a rare pink-skinned Muscat, the grapes of Moscatel de Setúbal.

grapes.name: Sercial, Verdelho, Boal, Malvasia, Terrantez
grapes.note: The noble white varieties of Madeira, which also define the wine's sweetness level when named on the label.

grapes.name: Verdelho (Azores)
grapes.note: The historic grape of Pico and Terceira, together with Arinto dos Açores and Terrantez do Pico.

countries.name: Cape Verde
countries.tagline: Wine from inside a live volcano: the vineyards of Chã das Caldeiras, in the crater of Pico do Fogo.

stats.note: No OIV figures. About 1.2 km2 of vines in the Fogo caldera (Wikipedia, Chã das Caldeiras); the Chã cooperative alone made about 100,000 litres a year by 2025 (Forbes África Lusófona, Aug 2025); a 2019 report claimed far more, so the area figure is uncertain.

countries.overview:
Cape Verde's wine comes almost entirely from one extraordinary place: Chã das Caldeiras, a flat-floored caldera about 9 km across at roughly 1,700 metres on the island of Fogo, overlooked by the 2,829 m cone of Pico do Fogo. Vines grow there in black volcanic ash and lapilli, planted in hollows dug down to moisture and spread low across the ground. Rain is scarce and erratic, but altitude and cool nights let the grapes keep their freshness in a country that sits at 15 degrees north.

Tradition credits a French count, François Louis Armand de Montrond, who stopped on Fogo around 1670, with introducing vines; Portuguese settlers certainly grew grapes on the island from the 17th century, and families in the crater still make a rustic house wine called *manecom*. Commercial bottling only began in 1998, when an Italian NGO helped organise a growers' cooperative and the *Chã* brand. The 2014 to 2015 eruption, the latest of many, buried most of the villages of Portela and Bangaeira and the old cooperative winery under lava, yet growers returned and rebuilt inside the crater.

Today the main labels are Chã (the cooperative, white, red and rosé, about 100,000 litres a year), Maria Chaves from the Monte Barro winery (a 25-hectare irrigated vineyard planted in 2009 with support from Capuchin-linked Italian aid), Sodade and Monte Losna. The whites, often from a Muscat-like local grape called *sabro branco*, are the best known; the reds lean on Alfrocheiro and Preta. There is no legally protected appellation yet.

history.title: Montrond's vines
history.text: Local tradition credits the French count Montrond, who stayed on Fogo after a voyage to Brazil, with bringing the first vines and coffee plants to the island.

history.title: The Chã cooperative
history.text: With support from the Italian NGO COSPE, growers began bottling wine commercially under the Chã label, the first modern Cape Verdean wine brand.

history.title: Eruption
history.text: The eruption that began on 23 November 2014 destroyed about three quarters of the buildings in Portela and Bangaeira, including the cooperative winery. A new winery opened inside the crater in 2015.

countries.classification: Cape Verde has no wine appellation system or OIV membership-based statistics. Wines are labelled by brand and island (Fogo).
countries.climate_soils: Tropical arid Sahelian climate moderated by altitude: vineyards in Chã das Caldeiras lie at about 1,600 to 1,900 m (some up to 2,100 m on the cone's flanks), on fresh volcanic ash, lapilli and lava fields with very little rain, which falls mainly between August and October. Vines are planted in hollows and trained low or as bush vines; dry farming is the norm except at the irrigated Maria Chaves vineyard.

grapes.name: Sabro branco
grapes.note: A Muscat-like local white grape, basis of the aromatic Fogo whites.

grapes.name: Alfrocheiro
grapes.note: Portuguese red variety that is now important for Fogo reds.

grapes.name: Preta tinta
grapes.note: Local name for the traditional red grapes used in manecom.

regions.name: Fogo
regions.tagline: Vines on fresh lava at 1,700 metres, inside the crater of Pico do Fogo.
regions.summary: Fogo ('fire') is the volcanic island of the Sotavento group, and its wine is grown almost entirely on the floor of the Chã das Caldeiras caldera beneath Pico do Fogo. The vines are low bushes in ash and cinder; the wines (mostly whites) are fresh, aromatic and saline, with surprising acidity for the latitude.
regions.history: Vines were introduced in the 17th century, traditionally by the Count of Montrond around 1670. For three centuries wine was a household product (manecom). Bottling began with the Chã cooperative in 1998; the Maria Chaves project followed in 2009 and released its first wine in 2013. The 1951, 1995 and 2014 eruptions repeatedly destroyed homes and vineyards, and each time the farmers came back.
regions.terroir: Altitude (about 1,700 m), strong sun, a short rainy season and young volcanic soils with almost no organic matter. The caldera wall (Bordeira) shelters the plain from the north-east trades; nights are cool enough to preserve acidity. Water is the limiting factor: harvests swing widely with the rains.
regions.grapes: Sabro branco (Muscat type), Alfrocheiro, local reds known as Preta; about 25 varieties were identified in a recent survey.
regions.styles: Dry whites (about three quarters of output), reds around 14% alcohol, rosé, a sparkling pilot and fruit liqueurs; manecom is the traditional sweetish house wine.

regions.name: Douro Valley
regions.tagline: A river carved through schist, terraced by hand over three centuries: the home of Port and of Portugal's most powerful red wines.
regions.summary:
The Douro Demarcated Region follows the river for about 100 km from Barqueiros, an hour east of Porto, to the Spanish border at Barca d'Alva. It covers some 250,000 hectares, of which roughly 43,000 to 44,000 are vineyard, farmed by about 18,000 growers. Almost all of it is mountain viticulture: the Douro is often described as holding around half of the world's steep-slope vineyard, and nearly every vine stands on a terrace someone built.

One territory carries two protected names. Porto (Port) is the fortified wine, made under an annual quota, the beneficio, that decides how much of each farm's must may be turned into Port. Douro is the name for everything else: dry reds and whites, rosés, sparkling wines and the fortified Moscatel do Douro. For two centuries the region was a grape farm for the Port shippers of Vila Nova de Gaia; since the 1990s it has become one of Europe's most exciting table-wine regions as well, with old-vine field blends from the side valleys of the Pinhão, Torto, Tua and Távora and a new generation of fresh whites from high-altitude vineyards.

The Alto Douro Wine Region, a 24,600 ha core of the demarcated area, was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list in 2001 as a cultural landscape. 2026 marks its 25th anniversary, and a difficult one: Port sales are shrinking, the region has more vines than the market needs, and growers' incomes depend on a quota system that many in the trade want reformed.
regions.history:
Wine was made here in Roman times, and the monasteries of the Middle Ages (Cistercians at Salzedas and São João de Tarouca on the south bank) kept it going. The English trade began in earnest in the late 17th century, when merchants who had been shipping thin red 'Viana' wine from the Minho discovered the richer wines of the upper Douro, and learned that a dose of brandy kept them sound on the voyage. The Methuen Treaty of 1703 gave Portuguese wine a lower tariff in England than French wine and turned Port into a national habit.

Boom brought fraud. After prices collapsed in the 1750s, the Marquis of Pombal created the Companhia Geral da Agricultura das Vinhas do Alto Douro (royal charter of 10 September 1756), drew a boundary around the vineyards, classified them, and between 1758 and 1761 set 335 granite marker stones along the limits of the best land. Wine from inside them was vinho de feitoria, fit for export; the rest was vinho de ramo, for the home market. It was one of the first legal delimitations of a wine region anywhere, and the Museu do Douro has located 105 of the original stones.

The 19th century brought the rabelo boats racing barrels down the rapids to Gaia, the blasting of the Cachão da Valeira gorge (1780 to 1792) that opened the upper river, Baron Forrester's maps and campaigns, the commanding figure of Dona Antónia Adelaide Ferreira, the arrival of the railway (Pinhão 1880, Barca d'Alva 1887), and then disaster: oidium in the 1850s and phylloxera from the 1860s. Replanting pushed vineyards east into the Douro Superior.

The 20th century was the age of regulation: the Casa do Douro (1932) and the Instituto do Vinho do Porto (1933), the vineyard points system devised by Álvaro Moreira da Fonseca in the late 1940s, and a rule that Port had to be shipped from the entreposto of Vila Nova de Gaia. In 1986, with EU accession, that monopoly ended and single estates could bottle and export their own Port. In 1952 Ferreira's winemaker Fernando Nicolau de Almeida made the first Barca Velha, proof that the Douro could produce a great dry red; in the 1990s and 2000s a wave of estates followed. The IVDP, created in 2003 from the old Port institute, now regulates both Porto and Douro.
regions.terroir:
The key is schist. The Douro's core is a band of Precambrian and Cambrian schist (the Douro-Beiras complex) set between granite on either side; Port vineyards are concentrated on the schist because its vertical, flaky layers let roots go metres deep in search of water, and because the stony surface stores and reflects heat. Where the granite begins, the quality ratings fall. Before planting, the rock is broken up, by hand with crowbars and explosives in the past and by bulldozers today, to create soil at all.

Climate grows hotter and drier upstream. The Serra do Marão shields the valley from Atlantic rain: Régua in the Baixo Corgo gets about 900 mm a year, Pinhão in the Cima Corgo around 650 to 700 mm, and Barca d'Alva on the Spanish border barely 400 mm. Summer days in the Douro Superior routinely pass 40 °C. Aspect and altitude matter enormously: the points system gives the most credit to south-facing slopes below 300 m close to the river, but in a warming climate growers are looking uphill and to north-facing sites for freshness, especially for whites.

Terraces shape every wine. The oldest are socalcos, narrow terraces held up by dry-stone walls, many rebuilt after phylloxera; the ruined, abandoned ones are called mortórios. From the 1970s the PDRITM development programme bulldozed wider earth-banked terraces, patamares, holding one or two rows and allowing small tractors. Vinha ao alto, rows planted straight up and down the slope, works where the gradient is below about 35 to 40 percent. Each system changes vine density, exposure, erosion and labour costs, and many quintas mix all three.
regions.grapes: More than 100 varieties are authorised. The historic vineyards are field blends, often with dozens of varieties interplanted. A 1981 study by José Ramos Pinto Rosas and João Nicolau de Almeida identified five as the best for Port, and they now dominate modern planting: Touriga Nacional (perfume, structure), Touriga Franca (the most planted, floral and dependable), Tinta Roriz (Tempranillo), Tinta Barroca (sweet, early ripening, for cooler sites) and Tinto Cão (late, fresh, fine-grained). Sousão is valued for colour and acidity, Tinta Amarela for spice. The whites are Malvasia Fina, Viosinho, Rabigato, Gouveio (Godello), Códega do Larinho and, for Moscatel do Douro, Moscatel Galego Branco.
regions.styles: Port: ruby styles (Ruby, Reserve, Late Bottled Vintage, Crusted, Vintage), wood-aged tawny styles (Tawny, Reserve Tawny, tawnies with an indication of age, Colheita), white Port and rosé Port. Douro DOC: full, dark reds from field blends and Touriga-based cuvées; mineral whites from high vineyards; rosés; traditional-method sparkling; Moscatel do Douro. IGP Duriense covers wines from the same area made outside DOC rules.
regions.classification:
The beneficio is the heart of the system. Every vineyard plot in the region is recorded in a register (the cadastro, kept by the Casa do Douro until 2004 and by the IVDP since) and scored on Moreira da Fonseca's method: location and subregion, altitude, slope, aspect and shelter, soil (schist scores, granite largely does not), proximity to the river, grape varieties, vine age, training and planting density, and yield. The total points place each parcel in a class from A (above 1,200 points) through B (1,001 to 1,200), C (801 to 1,000), D (601 to 800), E (401 to 600) to F (201 to 400). Each July the IVDP's interprofessional council fixes the region's total Port quota in pipas of 550 litres of fortified must, and that total is shared out by class, so an A-grade parcel can turn far more of its grapes into Port than an F-grade one.

The quota is what makes a Douro grape valuable: in 2026 Port grapes sold for roughly 900 to 1,200 euros a pipa, while grapes destined for Douro DOC wine fetched 150 to 400 euros. Shrinking sales forced cuts from 104,000 pipas in 2023 to 90,000 in 2024 and 75,000 in 2025; the 2026 harvest was set at 76,000 pipas (about 57 million kg of grapes). Port shippers such as the Fladgate Partnership argue the system stops them using the best grapes; growers defend it as their guaranteed income.

Port categories are defined by the IVDP's 2022 regulation (Regulamento 3/2022) and later council decisions; Douro DOC wines can carry Reserva, Grande Reserva, Colheita Tardia, Palhete and Clarete among other traditional terms.

regions.name: Madeira
regions.tagline: A volcanic island 1,000 km out in the Atlantic whose wine is deliberately heated and oxidised, and is all but indestructible.
regions.summary:
Madeira is the wine that cannot die. It is fortified, then heated for months or aged for decades in warm lofts, exposed to air on purpose, so that by the time it is bottled nothing is left that oxygen or heat can harm. A bottle from the 1790s can still be vibrant, and an opened bottle keeps for months. The flavours are unlike any other wine: burnt sugar, walnut, dried orange, coffee, smoke and iodine, carried by a searing acidity that keeps even the sweetest Malmsey from cloying.

The vineyards are tiny and vertiginous. About 400 hectares of vines, spread among roughly 1,200 growers, cling to terraces (poios) cut into the island's basalt, many trained on low pergolas (latada) so that vegetables can grow underneath, and watered by the levadas, the 600-year-old irrigation channels that thread the mountains. Harvest is by hand, and grapes are often carried down in baskets.

Trade is concentrated in a handful of shippers in Funchal and Câmara de Lobos. In 2025 they sold about 3.1 million litres for 20.6 million euros (IVBAM data): France is the largest market, followed by Germany, Belgium, the United States, the UK and Japan. Most of it is young, estufa-heated wine for cooking and everyday drinking; the treasures are the old Frasqueiras and the age-dated blends.
regions.history:
Madeira was settled from 1420 under the patronage of Prince Henry the Navigator, who had sugar cane and Malvasia vines brought from Crete and the eastern Mediterranean. The island sat on the sea routes to Africa, Brazil, the West Indies and India, and its wine became the ship's provision of choice. Shippers noticed that wine which had crossed the Equator twice in a ship's hold came back better than it left: the vinho da roda ('wine of the round voyage') commanded a premium, and by the late 18th century producers were imitating the voyage on land with heated stores (estufas, first recorded around 1794) and warm attic lodges.

A 1665 English law that banned European goods from being shipped to the American colonies except via England made an exception for Madeira, and the wine became the drink of colonial America. It was served at the signing celebrations of the Declaration of Independence in 1776; George Washington drank a pint a day at dinner; Thomas Jefferson ordered it by the pipe. British merchants (Blandy, Cossart Gordon, Leacock, Rutherford) ran the trade from Funchal.

Then the 19th century fell apart. Oidium arrived in 1852 and destroyed most of the vineyards; phylloxera followed from 1872. Many growers turned to sugar cane or replanted with American hybrids, and the noble varieties shrank to a fraction of their former area, while Tinta Negra became the workhorse. The American market collapsed with the Civil War and Prohibition, and the Russian market with the 1917 revolution. To survive, shippers merged: the Madeira Wine Association was formed in 1913, later becoming the Madeira Wine Company, which Blandy's joined in 1925. In 1989 the Blandys brought in the Symingtons as partners; in 2011 the Blandy family regained control, with the Symingtons keeping a minority share, and Chris Blandy, of the seventh generation, now leads it.

Since the 1990s and particularly since 2015, when new statutes reorganised the categories, Madeira has regained prestige among sommeliers and collectors. The old Frasqueiras of Barbeito, D'Oliveiras and Blandy's sell out, and Tinta Negra can now be named on labels, which has encouraged shippers to make fine wines from it.
regions.terroir:
Madeira is the top of a volcano rising from the ocean floor to 1,862 m at Pico Ruivo. Soils are basaltic and tuffaceous, acidic, rich in iron and magnesium, and very fertile when water is available. The climate is subtropical and maritime: warm all year in Funchal, but rain, mist and wind vary dramatically with aspect and altitude. The south coast (Câmara de Lobos, Estreito de Câmara de Lobos, Campanário, Funchal) is sunny and warm, with vines from sea level to about 700 m; Estreito and Jardim da Serra above Câmara de Lobos are the heartland of Sercial and Tinta Negra. The north (São Vicente, Seixal, Porto Moniz, Santana, Arco de São Jorge) is wetter, greener and cooler, home to Sercial and Verdelho, with vines sheltered from the trade winds by hedges of heather and fern. Porto Santo, the flat, dry neighbouring island, has sandy limestone soils and a small vineyard of Caracol and Listrão.

Humidity means rot and mildew pressure, which is why vines are trained high on pergolas or, in newer plantings, on espaliers (espaldeira). Natural acidity is very high, and that acidity is what makes Madeira able to survive heat and oxygen for centuries.
regions.grapes: The four classic white 'noble' varieties name both a grape and a sweetness level. Sercial (Esgana Cão) grows highest and coolest and makes the driest, most piercing wine; Verdelho is medium-dry and smoky; Boal (Bual, Boal Cachudo) is medium-sweet and raisined; Malvasia (Malmsey, mostly Malvasia de São Jorge and the historic Malvasia Cândida) is sweet, rich and still bracingly acid. Terrantez, nearly lost after oidium, is prized by collectors for a bittersweet balance between Verdelho and Boal; Bastardo is a rare red. Tinta Negra (formerly called Tinta Negra Mole) is the workhorse, the majority of production (about 60% or more of grapes on most estimates), used in every sweetness level. Listrão and Caracol are Porto Santo specialities; Moscatel and Complexa appear in small amounts.
regions.styles: By sweetness (in degrees Baumé): Seco (dry, up to 1.5°; Extra Seco below 0.5°), Meio Seco, Meio Doce and Doce (above 3.5°). A wine labelled Sercial must be dry or extra dry, Verdelho medium dry, Boal medium sweet, Malvasia sweet, and Terrantez medium dry or medium sweet. Rainwater is a lighter, pale style up to 10 years old. Madeirense DOP covers the island's unfortified table wines, and Terras Madeirenses IGP the rest.
regions.classification:
Production is controlled by the IVBAM (Instituto do Vinho, do Bordado e do Artesanato da Madeira) under statutes of 2015 (Portarias 38 to 40/2015). Two ways of ageing are recognised. Estufagem: fortified wine is held in tanks or casks warmed to no more than 50 °C (in practice 45 to 50 °C) for at least three months, then rested; it cannot be bottled before 31 October of the second year after harvest. Canteiro: wine is aged in casks stacked on wooden beams (canteiros) in warm lofts, heated only by the sun, for at least two years in wood and three before bottling; all the finest Madeira is canteiro.

Age-indicated blends: 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 40, 50 and More than 50 years old (the 2015 statute added 50 and More than 50), with traditional equivalents such as Reserva (5), Reserva Especial or Velha (10) and Reserva Extra (15); Seleccionado or Finest is the basic 3-year level. Single-vintage wines: Colheita (at least 5 years in wood, labelled with harvest and bottling dates) and Frasqueira or Garrafeira (at least 20 years in wood, from one recommended variety, exceptional quality, with bottling date); many great Frasqueiras spend 50 or 100 years in cask. Solera: a canteiro wine from a single vintage and variety, at least 5 years old, refreshed with up to 10% younger wine a year for at most ten additions.

Fortification is with neutral grape spirit of about 96% alcohol, to 17 to 22% abv. Wine for Madeira DOP can be fortified during fermentation (to keep sweetness) or after (for dry styles).

regions.name: Vinho Verde
regions.tagline: Portugal's green, rain-soaked north-west, where granite, Atlantic air and high-trained vines make some of Europe's freshest whites.
regions.summary:
The Vinho Verde region covers the whole north-west of Portugal, from the Minho river on the Spanish border south to the Douro and inland to the mountains: one of the largest demarcated regions in Europe, with just over 23,000 ha of vines in 2024 spread among tens of thousands of small farms. 'Verde' means green, and refers to youth and to the landscape, not the colour of the wine: there are red, rosé and sparkling Vinhos Verdes as well as white.

The style most foreigners know, a light, low-alcohol, slightly spritzy white sold in a squat bottle, was largely a creation of the 1950s to 1980s export trade. The modern region is far more interesting: single-variety Alvarinhos from Monção e Melgaço that age for a decade, Loureiro from the Lima valley smelling of laurel and orange blossom, Avesso from the warm Baião slopes near the Douro, and a new wave of skin-contact and old-vine wines from the mountain valleys. Reds from Vinhão, inky and acidic, remain a local passion, served in white porcelain bowls with roast pork and cod.
regions.history:
Vines were trained up trees here since Roman times, and medieval monasteries spread viticulture through the valleys. Minho red wine was the first Portuguese wine shipped in quantity to England from Viana do Castelo in the 14th to 17th centuries, until the merchants moved south to the Douro. The region was demarcated in 1908. For most of the 20th century vines grew on the edges of fields of maize and vegetables, trained high on trees (enforcado), pergolas (ramada) or tall cruzetas, so the ground beneath could be cropped: that is why Vinho Verde was historically light, acidic and high-yielding. Since the 1980s, EU-funded replanting moved most production to dedicated vineyards on lower cordon systems, and quality rose sharply.

The Comissão de Viticultura da Região dos Vinhos Verdes (CVRVV), founded in 1926, is one of the oldest regional wine commissions in Portugal. A long fight over the Alvarinho name ended with Portaria 152/2015: Monção e Melgaço kept exclusive use of 'Alvarinho' on Vinho Verde labels until 2021, after which any of the nine subregions may label a varietal Alvarinho, while Monção e Melgaço got its own seal and promotion.
regions.terroir: Granite almost everywhere, with some schist inland: sandy, acidic, free-draining soils. The climate is the wettest in Portugal (1,200 to 2,000 mm a year, falling mostly in winter and spring) and mild, thanks to the Atlantic, which pushes up the river valleys (Minho, Lima, Cávado, Ave, Douro). Inland subregions behind the first mountain ridges (Monção e Melgaço, Basto, Baião, Amarante) are drier and warmer in summer, allowing riper Alvarinho, Avesso and reds. Disease pressure is the constant challenge.
regions.grapes: Whites: Alvarinho, Loureiro, Arinto (here called Pedernã), Trajadura, Avesso, Azal. Reds: Vinhão (a teinturier with red flesh), Borraçal, Espadeiro (mostly for rosé), Amaral, Padeiro, Alvarelhão.
regions.styles: Crisp dry and off-dry whites, often with a light prickle; serious varietal Alvarinho and Loureiro; Vinho Verde Tinto; rosé; traditional-method sparkling (Espumante); Aguardente.
regions.classification: One DOC, Vinho Verde, with nine subregions that may appear on labels: Monção e Melgaço, Lima, Cávado, Ave, Basto, Sousa, Amarante, Baião and Paiva. IGP Minho covers the same area for wines outside the DOC rules, including international varieties. Since 2022, varietal Alvarinho can be labelled Vinho Verde Alvarinho in any subregion.

regions.name: Trás-os-Montes
regions.tagline: 'Behind the mountains': a remote, high, continental corner of north-east Portugal with old field blends and sharp, mountain-fresh wines.
regions.summary: Trás-os-Montes lies north of the Douro valley and east of the Marão and Alvão mountains, a land of chestnut forests, granite villages and harsh winters ('nine months of winter and three of hell', goes the saying). Most of its vineyard is small, old and cooperative-farmed; the area fell from about 23,000 ha in 2014 to about 4,565 ha in 2024 as abandonment and reclassification took their toll. Quality is uneven, but old field blends from Valpaços and the Planalto Mirandês are drawing interest from natural-wine makers.
regions.history: Vines were planted here by the Romans and by medieval monasteries; Chaves was the Roman Aquae Flaviae. The DOC dates from 2006, consolidating three earlier IPRs (Chaves, Valpaços and Planalto Mirandês). The region is the traditional home of the rustic palhete (light red made from mixed red and white grapes) and the warming, sweet 'vinho dos mortos' of Boticas, buried underground during the Napoleonic invasions and still made today.
regions.terroir: Granite and schist at 350 to 700 m; continental climate with hot summers, cold winters and around 600 mm of rain. The Planalto Mirandês on the Spanish border is the highest and harshest.
regions.grapes: Reds: Bastardo, Marufo, Tinta Roriz, Touriga Nacional, Trincadeira, Tinta Carvalha. Whites: Côdega do Larinho, Fernão Pires, Gouveio, Malvasia Fina, Rabigato, Síria, Viosinho.
regions.styles: Reds, field-blend palhetes, whites, sparkling and fortified (vinho licoroso).
regions.classification: DOC Trás-os-Montes with three subregions (Chaves, Valpaços, Planalto Mirandês); IGP Transmontano for the wider area.

regions.name: Távora-Varosa
regions.tagline: Portugal's first region demarcated for sparkling wine, on high Cistercian land south of the Douro.
regions.summary: A small mountain region on the plateau south of the Douro, between the Távora and Varosa rivers, at 500 to 800 m. Its cool, late-ripening vineyards and granite soils produce high-acid base wines, and the region is best known for traditional-method sparkling wine (Espumante), led by Murganheira and Raposeira. It was the first Portuguese region demarcated specifically for sparkling wine (as Varosa IPR in 1989, later promoted to DOC, absorbing the Encostas da Nave IPR).
regions.history: Cistercian monks arrived in the 12th century, founding São João de Tarouca (the first Cistercian monastery in Portugal) and Santa Maria de Salzedas, and planted vineyards; the IGP name Terras de Cister honours them. Raposeira near Lamego has made sparkling wine since 1898; Murganheira, founded in 1947, ages its wines in tunnels carved into the granite.
regions.terroir: Granite and some schist, 500 to 800 m; cold winters, cool nights and late harvests that keep acidity high.
regions.grapes: Malvasia Fina, Cerceal, Gouveio, Bical, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Pinot Blanc; Touriga Nacional, Tinta Roriz.
regions.styles: Traditional-method sparkling wines (white and rosé), plus still whites and reds.
regions.classification: DOC Távora-Varosa; IGP Terras de Cister.

regions.name: Bairrada
regions.tagline: Clay, Atlantic air and the fearsome Baga grape: Portugal's Nebbiolo country, and its capital of sparkling wine and roast suckling pig.
regions.summary: Bairrada is a low, rolling strip between the Atlantic dunes and the Buçaco mountains, between Aveiro and Coimbra. Its name comes from barro, clay, and its identity from Baga, a thick-skinned, high-acid, very tannic red grape that, when properly ripened, makes some of the longest-lived wines in Portugal: dark cherry, plum, tobacco and earth, with Nebbiolo-like structure. It is also Portugal's sparkling-wine heartland, and Bairrada Espumante is the standard partner for leitão (roast suckling pig) at the restaurants of Mealhada. About 9,300 ha of vines remained in 2024, down by a third in a decade.
regions.history: Bairrada's wines were traded through Aveiro and Coimbra in the Middle Ages. In the 18th century Pombal ordered many vineyards uprooted to protect the Douro's reputation (Bairrada wine was being used to colour Port), and the region was only demarcated in 1979. The first sparkling wine was made around 1890 by the Escola Prática de Viticultura in Anadia, and the 20th-century caves (Caves São João, Aliança, Messias, Primavera) built the region's name on sparkling wine and long-aged red Garrafeiras. From the 1980s Luís Pato, his daughter Filipa and a group of growers, the Baga Friends, fought to rehabilitate Baga as a single-variety wine. In the mid-2010s the CVB introduced the Bairrada Clássico category for wines respecting traditional varieties and ageing, and a Baga Bairrada label for traditional-method sparkling wines made mainly from Baga.
regions.terroir: Clay-limestone (the best Baga sites) and sandy soils, gently rolling hills at 40 to 150 m; maritime climate, about 1,000 mm of rain, cool nights and frequent autumn rain that makes late-ripening Baga a gamble. Sandy soils give lighter wines and suit whites.
regions.grapes: Baga dominates the reds, with Touriga Nacional, Alfrocheiro, Castelão, Tinta Roriz, Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot. Whites: Maria Gomes (Fernão Pires), Bical, Cercial, Arinto, Sercialinho, Chardonnay.
regions.styles: Tannic, ageworthy reds; fresh whites; traditional-method sparkling (Espumante) in all colours.
regions.classification: DOC Bairrada (demarcated 1979), with the categories Bairrada Clássico and Baga Bairrada (sparkling); IGP Beira Atlântico.

regions.name: Dão
regions.tagline: A granite bowl ringed by mountains, the homeland of Touriga Nacional and of Portugal's most Burgundian reds and whites.
regions.summary: The Dão sits on a granite plateau in central Portugal, enclosed by the Caramulo, Buçaco and Serra da Estrela mountains, which block Atlantic rain from the west and continental extremes from the east. Vineyards are scattered in clearings among pine and eucalyptus forest at 400 to 700 m, and the wines are known for elegance rather than power: perfumed, mineral, fresh reds with fine tannins and textured, long-lived whites, especially from Encruzado. About 9,800 ha of vines remained in 2024, a third fewer than a decade earlier.
regions.history: Wine has been made around Viseu since Roman times; the Dão was demarcated in 1908, among the first table-wine regions in Portugal. Under the Estado Novo, rules from the 1950s channelled almost all Dão wine through cooperatives, which made dull, oxidised wine for decades. EU entry in 1986 ended the monopoly; Sogrape's Quinta dos Carvalhais, Quinta dos Roques, Álvaro Castro (Quinta da Pellada), Quinta da Falorca and others rebuilt the region's reputation. Touriga Nacional, native here, was revived through clonal selection from the 1970s and 1980s, with the Nelas research station among the pioneers.
regions.terroir: Granite (decomposed, sandy, acidic) with some schist in the south-west; altitude and mountain shelter give warm days and cool nights, about 1,100 mm of rain falling mostly in winter. The Serra da Estrela subregion, Portugal's highest vineyards (up to around 800 m), gives the freshest wines.
regions.grapes: Touriga Nacional, Alfrocheiro, Tinta Roriz (Aragonez), Jaen (Mencía), Tinto Cão, Baga; Encruzado, Malvasia Fina, Bical, Cercial, Verdelho.
regions.styles: Elegant, age-worthy reds; textured whites; rosé and sparkling (Dão Espumante).
regions.classification: DOC Dão (1908) with seven subregions (Alva, Besteiros, Castendo, Serra da Estrela, Silgueiros, Terras de Azurara, Terras de Senhorim); 'Dão Nobre' is a special top category requiring tasting panel approval; IGP Terras do Dão.

regions.name: Beira Interior
regions.tagline: Portugal's highest wine region, on the plateaux along the Spanish border, where old vines and altitude make taut, mineral wines.
regions.summary: Beira Interior runs north to south along the Spanish border, from the Douro to the Tejo, with the Serra da Estrela, Portugal's highest mainland mountain, at its western edge. Vineyards lie at 300 to 750 m, many of them old field blends farmed by cooperatives. Long under-rated, the region is now attracting producers looking for freshness in a warming climate: Rui Roboredo Madeira, Quinta dos Termos, Quinta do Cardo and newcomers in the Cova da Beira are making crisp Síria whites and fragrant Rufete and Touriga reds.
regions.history: Settled since prehistory (Côa rock art lies at its northern edge) and fortified through the Middle Ages, the Beira Interior was a land of castles and transhumance. Its three former IPRs, Castelo Rodrigo, Pinhel and Cova da Beira, were merged into DOC Beira Interior (EU registration 2004) and are now subregions.
regions.terroir: Granite and schist plateaux, some of the highest vineyards in Portugal; continental climate with very cold winters, hot dry summers and large day-night swings.
regions.grapes: Síria (Roupeiro), Fonte Cal, Arinto, Fernão Pires, Malvasia Fina; Rufete, Tinta Roriz, Touriga Nacional, Jaen, Marufo, Trincadeira.
regions.styles: Fresh whites, perfumed reds, sparkling wines (especially from Pinhel).
regions.classification: DOC Beira Interior with three subregions (Castelo Rodrigo, Pinhel, Cova da Beira); IGP Terras da Beira.

regions.name: Lisboa
regions.tagline: Windswept Atlantic hills north of the capital: once Portugal's bulk-wine engine, now a home of fresh whites, value reds and three historic oddities.
regions.summary: The Lisboa region (called Estremadura until 2008) runs along the Atlantic coast from Lisbon north to Leiria, about 18,000 ha of vines in 2024. Cool Atlantic winds and fog make it fresher than its latitude suggests. For centuries it supplied cheap wine to the capital and the colonies; today it is Portugal's biggest producer of Vinho Regional, with modern estates around Alenquer and a growing name for crisp whites and supple reds. On the Lisbon fringe survive three of Europe's most remarkable historic appellations: Bucelas (Arinto whites, 'Lisbon Hock'), Colares (ungrafted vines in Atlantic sand) and Carcavelos (a fortified wine nearly swallowed by suburbs).
regions.history: Colares and Carcavelos were demarcated in 1907 and 1908 and Bucelas in 1911, among the first in Portugal. The rest of the region was a sea of cooperatives until the 1980s and 1990s, when estates such as Quinta do Monte d'Oiro, Quinta de Chocapalha, Quinta da Romeira and Casa Santos Lima showed what the Atlantic hills could do.
regions.terroir: Limestone, clay and sandstone hills, rarely above 400 m (Serra de Montejunto at 666 m is the highest point), whipped by Atlantic winds that cool the vines and limit disease. Colares is pure dune sand over clay; Bucelas is limestone and clay in a sheltered valley; Carcavelos is limestone and clay by the Tejo estuary.
regions.grapes: Arinto, Fernão Pires, Vital, Seara Nova, Malvasia, Chardonnay; Castelão, Tinta Roriz (Aragonez), Touriga Nacional, Syrah, Alicante Bouschet, Tinta Miúda; Ramisco in Colares.
regions.styles: Fresh whites, medium-bodied reds, rosé, sparkling, fortified (Carcavelos), and aguardente (Lourinhã).
regions.classification: Nine DOCs: Bucelas, Colares, Carcavelos, Alenquer, Arruda, Óbidos, Torres Vedras, Lourinhã (aguardente only) and Encostas d'Aire (shared with the Tejo border area). IGP Lisboa covers the wider area, with mentions such as Estremadura, Alta Estremadura and Lisboa Estremadura.

regions.name: Tejo
regions.tagline: Portugal's breadbasket on the banks of the Tagus, where fertile floodplains meet sandy heaths and limestone hills.
regions.summary: The Tejo region (Ribatejo until 2009) follows the river Tagus north-east of Lisbon through Santarém, Almeirim, Cartaxo, Chamusca and Tomar. About 12,000 ha of vines in 2024 grow in three very different landscapes: the fertile alluvial floodplain (lezíria or campo), the sandy heaths south of the river (charneca), and the clay-limestone hills north of it (bairro). Historically a source of bulk wine, the Tejo now makes good-value reds and whites, with a few serious estates.
regions.history: Royal estates and religious orders farmed the Tagus valley since the Middle Ages; the Templars at Tomar and the kings at Almeirim had vineyards. The Ribatejo was demarcated as an IPR in the 1980s with six subregions (Almeirim, Cartaxo, Chamusca, Coruche, Santarém, Tomar), merged into a single DOC Do Tejo (EU name DoTejo, 2011).
regions.terroir: Campo: fertile alluvium, high yields, lighter wines. Bairro: clay-limestone hills, the best reds. Charneca: poor, sandy soils, hot and dry, good for concentrated reds and Fernão Pires.
regions.grapes: Fernão Pires (the regional white), Arinto, Talia, Verdelho; Castelão, Trincadeira, Touriga Nacional, Tinta Roriz, Alicante Bouschet, Syrah, Cabernet Sauvignon.
regions.styles: Aromatic Fernão Pires whites, fruity reds, rosé, sparkling, late-harvest and fortified.
regions.classification: DOC DoTejo (registered 2011; the six former subregions are no longer used); IGP Tejo for the wider area.

regions.name: Península de Setúbal
regions.tagline: Muscat country south of Lisbon: amber Moscatel de Setúbal from the Arrábida hills and supple Castelão from the sandy plain.
regions.summary: Across the Tagus from Lisbon, the Setúbal Peninsula has two faces. The limestone Serra da Arrábida, rising straight from the sea, shelters vineyards around Azeitão and Palmela that grow Muscat for Moscatel de Setúbal, Portugal's great sweet fortified white. Inland, the vast sandy plain toward Pegões and Poceirão is Castelão country, producing soft, red-fruited reds in large volumes. The region is home to two of Portugal's biggest family wine companies, José Maria da Fonseca and Bacalhôa, and to Casa Ermelinda Freitas.
regions.history: Moscatel from Setúbal was exported from the 14th century, and the Setúbal DOC is among Portugal's oldest (demarcated 1907). José Maria da Fonseca, founded in 1834 in Vila Nogueira de Azeitão, made the Periquita red one of Portugal's first wine brands and still ages Moscatel stocks back to the 19th century. Bacalhôa takes its name from a 15th-century palace and estate bought by the Berardo group, whose collection of modern art and tiles is shown at the winery.
regions.terroir: Arrábida: limestone and clay slopes, protected from Atlantic winds, warm and humid near the sea. The plain: deep, poor, sandy soils (podzols) with hot summers, where Castelão ripens easily.
regions.grapes: Moscatel de Setúbal (Muscat of Alexandria, Moscatel Graúdo), Moscatel Roxo; Castelão; Fernão Pires, Arinto, Antão Vaz; Syrah, Alicante Bouschet, Touriga Nacional, Aragonez.
regions.styles: Moscatel de Setúbal and Moscatel Roxo (fortified), Castelão reds, whites, rosés and sparkling wines.
regions.classification: DOC Setúbal (fortified Moscatel), DOC Palmela (table wines and fortified), IGP Península de Setúbal.

regions.name: Alentejo
regions.tagline: Big skies, cork oaks and marble towns: Portugal's favourite wine region, and the last place in Europe where wine is still routinely made in Roman-style clay jars.
regions.summary: The Alentejo ('beyond the Tejo') covers almost a third of mainland Portugal: rolling plains of wheat, olive groves and cork-oak montado, with low hills and whitewashed towns. Once a cereal belt, it became the country's most popular wine region from the 1990s, prized at home for ripe, generous, fruit-forward reds that are easy to love young. It is also the only Portuguese region that grew in the last decade, to about 26,000 ha in 2024, more than double its 1989 area. Large estates (herdades) with irrigation coexist with cooperatives and a growing number of small, fresh-styled producers in the cooler Portalegre hills.
regions.history: The Romans made wine here in talhas, huge clay amphorae, and villas such as São Cucufate near Vidigueira had their own presses. The tradition of talha wine survived in villages around Vidigueira, Vila de Frades and Cuba. In the 20th century the Estado Novo's wheat campaign uprooted vineyards; the post-1974 land reform and then EU accession in 1986 reshaped the countryside. Herdade do Esporão (from 1985), the Cartuxa foundation in Évora and the cooperatives of Reguengos, Borba and Redondo led a quality revolution. The CVR Alentejana was founded in 1989; the subregions were recognised as IPRs in the 1980s and unified under DOC Alentejo, and Vinho de Talha DOC Alentejo was recognised in 2010. The Alentejo's Wine Sustainability Programme (2015) has made it a leader in certified sustainable viticulture.
regions.terroir: Mediterranean-continental: very hot, dry summers (40 °C is common), mild winters, 500 to 700 mm of rain. Soils vary: schist (Reguengos, Granja-Amareleja, Vidigueira), granite (Portalegre), marble and limestone around Estremoz and Borba, clays and Mediterranean red soils elsewhere. The Serra de São Mamede around Portalegre, rising to over 1,000 m, gives the freshest wines; the Vidigueira fault scarp funnels Atlantic air over the vineyards to the south.
regions.grapes: Reds: Aragonez (Tinta Roriz), Trincadeira, Alicante Bouschet, Castelão, Touriga Nacional, Syrah, Tinta Grossa, Moreto. Whites: Antão Vaz, Roupeiro (Síria), Arinto, Fernão Pires, Rabo de Ovelha, Manteúdo, Perrum, Diagalves.
regions.styles: Ripe reds, whites from Antão Vaz and Arinto, rosé, sparkling, and Vinho de Talha (amphora wine).
regions.classification: DOC Alentejo, with eight subregions that may be named on the label: Portalegre, Borba, Redondo, Reguengos, Vidigueira, Évora, Granja-Amareleja and Moura. 'Vinho de Talha DOC Alentejo' designates wines fermented and kept in clay talhas. Most wine is sold as IGP Alentejano.

regions.name: Algarve
regions.tagline: Portugal's sunny southern coast, where a small wine revival is growing between the golf courses.
regions.summary: The Algarve is better known for beaches than wine, but vines have grown here since Phoenician and Roman times, and the region has four DOCs: Lagos, Portimão, Lagoa and Tavira. For decades the local cooperatives made heavy, alcoholic reds; since the 2000s a few dozen estates (some owned by foreign investors and one by the singer Cliff Richard) have improved quality, with rosés, Negra Mole reds and fresh whites. Production fell 20% in 2025.
regions.history: Moorish rule (8th to 13th centuries) and later the fishing economy shaped the region; wine was a local product. The four DOCs were demarcated in the 1980s around the cooperatives of each town. Only the Lagoa cooperative remains significant, and many vineyards are sold under IGP Algarve.
regions.terroir: Mediterranean with Atlantic influence: hot, dry summers, mild winters. The Serra de Monchique and Serra do Caldeirão shelter the coastal strip from the north. Soils: sandy, red clays and limestone (barrocal).
regions.grapes: Negra Mole (the local red, pale and spicy), Castelão, Trincadeira, Touriga Nacional, Syrah, Aragonez, Alicante Bouschet; Arinto, Síria, Malvasia Fina, Moscatel Graúdo, Manteúdo, Crato Branco.
regions.styles: Reds, rosés, whites, some fortified and sparkling.
regions.classification: DOCs Lagos, Portimão, Lagoa and Tavira; IGP Algarve.

regions.name: Azores
regions.tagline: Mid-Atlantic volcanic islands where vines grow in black-stone pens beside the surf: Pico's UNESCO landscape and some of Europe's most saline whites.
regions.summary: The Azores lie 1,500 km west of Lisbon in the middle of the Atlantic. Three islands have DOCs: Pico, whose vineyards of tiny walled plots (currais) on black lava are a UNESCO World Heritage landscape; Biscoitos on Terceira; and Graciosa. For centuries their claim to fame was a fortified Verdelho that, the islanders say, reached the tables of the Russian tsars. Today the islands are famous among sommeliers for dry whites from Arinto dos Açores, Verdelho and Terrantez do Pico: high-acid, salty, smoky and quite unlike anything else. Production rebounded in 2025 (up 221% on a disastrous 2024), but volumes remain tiny.
regions.history: Franciscan friars are said to have brought Verdelho from Sicily (or Madeira) in the 15th century. Pico's Verdelho, fortified like Madeira, was exported to northern Europe, Brazil and Russia in the 18th and 19th centuries. Oidium (1850s) and phylloxera (1870s) wiped out the vineyards; American hybrid vines (for the local 'vinho de cheiro') replaced many of them. Revival began in the 1980s with the Pico cooperative and the DOCs (1994); UNESCO inscribed the Pico vineyard landscape in 2004. Since 2014 the Azores Wine Company (António Maçanita, Filipe Rocha, Paulo Machado) has led a new wave, replanting abandoned currais.
regions.terroir: Young basaltic lava (lajido, 'biscoitos'), barely weathered, with vines planted in cracks in the rock and protected by walls of piled black stone from salt-laden winds. Oceanic climate: mild, humid, windy, about 1,000 mm of rain on Pico's coast. Vineyards lie within about 100 m of sea level.
regions.grapes: Arinto dos Açores (distinct from mainland Arinto), Verdelho, Terrantez do Pico; also Boal, Sercial, Fernão Pires, Generosa, Malvasia; hybrids (Isabella) for vinho de cheiro.
regions.styles: Dry and fortified (licoroso) whites; some reds and rosés under IGP Açores.
regions.classification: DOCs Pico, Biscoitos and Graciosa (registered 1996); IGP Açores. The EU single document for Pico (2014) covers its fortified licoroso; dry still whites from the islands are widely bottled under IGP Açores or as DOC Pico according to the current regional rules.

appellations.name: Porto
match: Porto / Port / vinho do Porto / Port Wine / vin de Porto / Oporto / Portvin / Portwein / Portwijn
appellations.grapes: Touriga Franca, Touriga Nacional, Tinta Roriz, Tinta Barroca, Tinto Cão, Tinta Amarela, Sousão and dozens more in old field blends; for white Port, Malvasia Fina, Gouveio, Viosinho, Rabigato, Códega do Larinho
appellations.summary:
Port is a red (or white) wine whose fermentation is stopped part-way by adding grape spirit. Grapes are crushed and, at the best quintas, still trodden by foot in shallow granite tanks called lagares, because Port ferments for only two or three days and colour and tannin have to be extracted fast. When about half the sugar has turned to alcohol, the wine is run off onto aguardente vínica, a neutral grape brandy of about 77% alcohol: roughly 115 litres of spirit to 435 litres of must makes a 550-litre pipa. The yeasts die, the remaining sugar stays, and the wine ends up at 19 to 22% alcohol (white Port can be as low as 16.5%).

What happens next decides the style. Ruby Ports are aged in large vats or bottle to keep their dark fruit: basic Ruby; Reserve; Late Bottled Vintage (a single year bottled between the fourth and sixth year, a style pioneered by Taylor's with its 1965); Crusted (a bottle-aged blend of vintages); and Vintage Port, made only in the best years from the best lots, bottled unfiltered in its second or third year and built to age for decades. A shipper declares a vintage after the IVDP approves samples in the spring of the second year; famous general declarations include 1927, 1945, 1963, 1977, 1994, 2011, and the back-to-back 2016 and 2017. Single-quinta Vintage Ports (Vargellas, Malvedos, Cavadinha, Vesuvio) often come from the years in between.

Tawny Ports are aged in small, old casks (pipas, about 550 to 620 litres) where slow oxidation turns them amber, nutty and dried-fruited. A 10, 20, 30 or 40 Year Old Tawny is a blend whose taste matches that average age; the IVDP added 50 Years Old in 2021/22 and, by a circular of January 2025, an 80 Years Old indication plus Very Very Old (VVO) for unstated blends of 80 years or more. Colheita is a single-vintage tawny aged at least seven years in wood, labelled with harvest and bottling dates. White Port ranges from dry aperitif styles to aged whites with an indication of age, and rosé Port has been allowed since 2008.
appellations.terroir: Only the schist core of the valley, graded A to F under the beneficio, can supply Port. The Cima Corgo, around Pinhão and its side valleys, provides most Vintage Port; the Douro Superior gives increasingly important ripe, powerful wines; the Baixo Corgo, wetter and more fertile, supplies much of the ruby and young tawny. Most Port is still aged and blended in the lodges of Vila Nova de Gaia, where the cool, humid Atlantic air slows evaporation; wines aged up the valley take on a hotter, richer 'Douro bake'.
appellations.nerd_note: Vintage Port is the only great wine in the world normally released when it is two years old. A 'declaration' is a shipper's decision, not the IVDP's: the Institute only approves the samples, so in split years some houses declare and others make single-quinta wines instead.

appellations.name: Douro
appellations.created: 1756 (region); DOC for unfortified wines late 20th century
appellations.grapes: Touriga Nacional, Touriga Franca, Tinta Roriz, Tinta Barroca, Tinto Cão, Sousão, old-vine field blends; whites from Rabigato, Viosinho, Gouveio, Códega do Larinho, Malvasia Fina, Arinto; Moscatel Galego Branco for Moscatel do Douro
appellations.summary:
The Douro DOC covers the unfortified wines of the same demarcated region as Port, and for most of its history they were an afterthought: everyday reds for the farm, or the grapes that missed out on the Port quota. The exception that proved what was possible was Barca Velha, first made in 1952 by Fernando Nicolau de Almeida at Quinta do Vale Meão for A. A. Ferreira, using ice carried up the valley to cool the fermentation. It is released only in exceptional years (around twenty times since 1952) and remains Portugal's most famous red.

The real revolution came after 1986 and especially in the 1990s, when families who had sold grapes to Port shippers began bottling dry wines under their own names. The five estates that marketed themselves together from 2003 as the Douro Boys (Quinta do Crasto, Quinta do Vale Meão, Quinta do Vallado, Niepoort and Quinta Vale Dona Maria) became the face of that change. Today more than 60 million bottles of Douro DOC wine are sold a year, using over half of the region's grapes.

The classic Douro red is dark, dense and perfumed: Touriga Nacional's violets and bergamot, Touriga Franca's rose and black fruit, the grip of schist-grown tannin, often with the herbal, resinous note of the hillside scrub (esteva, rockrose). Old-vine field blends (vinhas velhas), sometimes with 30 or more varieties interplanted, give the most complex wines. Whites from high plateau vineyards around Alijó, Murça, Favaios and the Douro Superior's upper slopes are increasingly serious: taut, saline and long-lived. The DOC also covers Moscatel do Douro, rosés and traditional-method sparkling wine.
appellations.terroir: Same schist slopes and climate gradient as Port, but table-wine growers prize what the Port points system penalises: altitude (500 to 700 m for whites), north and east aspects, granite margins and old field-blend vineyards. The economic problem is that DOC grapes are worth far less than Port grapes, which pushes growers toward volume and has led to abandonment of steep plots.
appellations.nerd_note: Barca Velha is named after an old boat; the first vintage was cooled with blocks of ice brought from Porto, because Vale Meão had no electricity. When a year is good but not quite great enough, Casa Ferreirinha releases it as Reserva Especial instead.

appellations.name: Moscatel do Douro
appellations.grapes: Moscatel Galego Branco (Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains), at least 85%
appellations.summary: Moscatel do Douro is the Douro's other fortified wine: Muscat grapes, fortified with grape spirit like Port, at least 85% Moscatel and 16.5% alcohol or more, then aged at least 18 months in wood. Most of it comes from the high, cooler plateau around Favaios and Alijó, at roughly 500 to 600 m, where the small-berried Moscatel Galego keeps its acidity and its orange-blossom perfume. The village cooperative, Adega Cooperativa de Favaios, made the name so well known in Portugal that many people simply order 'a Favaios'. Aged versions (10 and 20 years, occasionally single-vintage) turn amber and develop notes of orange peel, honey and walnut.
appellations.terroir: Granite and schist plateau north of Pinhão, at the edge of the demarcated region; more Atlantic influence and cooler nights than the river valley.
appellations.nerd_note: A dash of Moscatel is also used by some shippers to lift the aroma of white Port blends.

appellations.name: Baixo Corgo
appellations.grapes: Touriga Franca, Tinta Roriz, Tinta Barroca, Touriga Nacional; whites Malvasia Fina, Gouveio
appellations.summary: The westernmost and smallest of the three subregions, from Barqueiros to the Corgo river at Peso da Régua and Lamego on the south bank. It is the wettest (around 900 mm of rain at Régua), greenest and most densely planted part of the Douro, about 14,000 ha of vines, with deeper soils and higher yields. Historically it supplied the bulk of young ruby and tawny Port; today it is also home to ambitious table-wine estates such as Quinta do Vallado, Quinta da Gaivosa and Quinta do Côtto, whose wines tend to be fresher and more elegant than those upstream.
appellations.terroir: Schist with granite outcrops; Atlantic influence through the Marão gap; many patamares and vinha ao alto plantings on gentler slopes.
producers: Casa de Mateus (Sogrape, IGP and DOC)
appellations.nerd_note: Peso da Régua was the river port where the Companhia's officials weighed and taxed the wine (peso means weight), and it is still the administrative capital of the region.

appellations.name: Cima Corgo
appellations.grapes: Touriga Franca, Touriga Nacional, Tinta Roriz, Tinto Cão, Tinta Barroca, Sousão, field blends
appellations.summary: The heart of Port: from the Corgo river east to the Cachão da Valeira gorge, centred on the village of Pinhão and the side valleys of the Pinhão, Torto, Tua and Távora. Around 19,000 ha of vines, almost all on steep schist, include most of the famous Vintage Port quintas: Noval, Roêda, Bomfim, Malvedos, Cavadinha, Panascal, Cruzeiro, Seixo, La Rosa, Vale Dona Maria. Rainfall is around 650 to 700 mm, summers are hot, and the many valleys give every possible aspect, which is why blenders draw on so many quintas here. It produces the bulk of the region's top-graded A and B vineyards.
appellations.terroir: Deep, hard schist; terraces of every era (pre-phylloxera socalcos, 1970s patamares, vinha ao alto); hot south-facing amphitheatres along the main river, cooler side-valley slopes.
appellations.nerd_note: Pombal's first boundary (marked out 1757 to 1761) covered roughly the Baixo Corgo and the western Cima Corgo; it crept east over the following decades, and the Douro Superior was only fully included in the early 20th century.

appellations.name: Douro Superior
appellations.grapes: Touriga Nacional, Touriga Franca, Tinta Roriz, Sousão; whites Rabigato, Códega do Larinho
appellations.summary: East of the Cachão da Valeira gorge to the Spanish border at Barca d'Alva: the largest subregion by land but with only about 8,700 ha of vines, because it was cut off by the rapids until the 1790s and remote until the railway reached it in 1887. It is the hottest and driest part of the Douro (around 400 mm of rain near the border), with flatter land that allows mechanisation, and it is where most new planting has happened since the 1980s. Great estates include Quinta de Vargellas (Taylor's), Quinta do Vesuvio (Symington), Quinta do Vale Meão (birthplace of Barca Velha) and Quinta da Leda (Casa Ferreirinha). Wines are riper, darker and fuller, with soft, generous tannins.
appellations.terroir: Schist and some granite; continental climate with very hot summers and cold winters; the Côa valley, with its Palaeolithic rock art, enters the Douro here.
appellations.nerd_note: Ramos Pinto's Quinta de Ervamoira was planted in the 1970s with Portugal's first large vinha ao alto vineyard, and the discovery of rock engravings nearby in the 1990s helped stop a dam that would have flooded it.

appellations.name: Duriense
appellations.grapes: Douro varieties plus international grapes
appellations.summary: The regional (IGP) designation for the Douro area, used for wines made outside DOC Douro rules: different varieties or blends, experimental styles, or wines a producer simply prefers not to submit to the DOC tasting panel. Some serious bottlings appear under it, but most Duriense wine is everyday drinking.
appellations.terroir: Same area as the Douro DOC.
appellations.nerd_note: Like the DOC, it is administered by the IVDP rather than a regional commission.

appellations.name: Madeira
match: Madeira / Vinho da Madeira / Madère / Vin de Madère / Madera / Madeira Wein / Madeira Wine / Vino di Madera / Madeira Wijn
appellations.created: Regulated from the early 20th century; DOP registered 1991; statute 2015
appellations.grapes: Tinta Negra (majority); noble whites Sercial, Verdelho, Boal, Malvasia (Malvasia de São Jorge, Malvasia Cândida), Terrantez; Bastardo, Moscatel, Complexa, Listrão
appellations.summary:
Madeira is the only wine region where heat and air, the two things that ruin every other wine, are the point of the process. Grapes are pressed and fermented, then fortified with grape spirit at around 96% to between 17 and 22% alcohol: early, during fermentation, for the sweet styles (Boal, Malvasia), and later for dry Sercial and Verdelho. The wine is then either warmed in an estufa (no more than 50 °C, at least three months) or, for every fine Madeira, left in casks in hot lofts (canteiro) for years or decades. The slow cooking and oxidation turn fruit into caramel, toffee, roasted nuts, marmalade, coffee and smoke, while Madeira's ferocious acidity keeps it alive.

The labels tell you three things. The grape, if named (85% minimum), fixes the sweetness: Sercial dry, Verdelho medium dry, Boal medium sweet, Malvasia sweet, Terrantez in between. The age: 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 40, 50 or More than 50 years for blends, or a vintage for Colheita (at least 5 years in wood) and Frasqueira (at least 20). And the house: Blandy's, Barbeito, D'Oliveiras, Henriques & Henriques, Justino's, Broadbent, Borges, Faria.

Great old Madeira is one of the longest-lived things you can drink. Wines from the 19th century, and occasionally the 18th, still appear at auction and are often in perfect condition, because there is nothing left in them to spoil. Once opened, a bottle lasts months.
appellations.terroir: Basalt terraces from sea level to about 800 m on the south coast and lower, cooler slopes on the north; very high natural acidity everywhere. The south (Câmara de Lobos, Estreito, Campanário) is warmer and supplies Tinta Negra, Boal and Malvasia; the north (São Vicente, Seixal, Porto Moniz, Santana) gives Sercial and Verdelho their tension.
appellations.nerd_note: Since 2015 Tinta Negra can be named on the label, and shippers now bottle 50-year-old Tinta Negra Colheitas that are as complex as noble-grape wines. The rule linking variety to sweetness can be waived for Frasqueiras with the IVBAM tasting panel's approval.

appellations.name: Madeirense
appellations.grapes: Verdelho, Sercial, Arnsburger, Malvasia, Boal, Tinta Negra, Aragonez, Touriga Nacional, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Bastardo and others
appellations.summary: The DOP for Madeira's unfortified table wines: whites from Verdelho, Sercial, Arnsburger and Malvasia, reds and rosés from Tinta Negra and mainland or international varieties. Volumes are small and mostly consumed on the island, but quality has improved fast; Atlantis rosé from the Madeira Wine Company and Verdelho-based whites from the north coast show sharp acidity and a salty edge. Sales of Madeirense DOP rose almost 24% in 2025.
appellations.terroir: Same basalt terraces as Madeira DOP; whites favour the cool, wet north coast (São Vicente, Seixal, Porto Moniz).
appellations.nerd_note: Arnsburger, a German Riesling crossing introduced in the 20th century, has become one of the island's typical table-wine whites.

appellations.name: Terras Madeirenses
appellations.grapes: Island varieties plus international grapes
appellations.summary: The regional wine designation for Madeira and Porto Santo, for wines outside the Madeirense DOP rules.
appellations.terroir: Madeira and Porto Santo.

appellations.name: Vinho Verde
appellations.grapes: Alvarinho, Loureiro, Arinto (Pedernã), Trajadura, Avesso, Azal; Vinhão, Borraçal, Espadeiro, Amaral
appellations.summary:
Vinho Verde is Portugal's biggest DOC by number of growers and one of its most exported: the classic is a white of 9 to 11.5% alcohol, bone-dry to off-dry, with lime, green apple and sea-breeze freshness and sometimes a faint sparkle, originally from malolactic fermentation in bottle and now usually from a little added carbon dioxide. It is the wine Portugal drinks with grilled sardines in June.

The serious end has transformed in a generation. Varietal Alvarinho from the warm, sheltered Monção e Melgaço subregion reaches 12.5 to 13.5%, with peach, citrus and saline minerality, and some, aged on lees or in large oak, need five or ten years. Loureiro from the Lima and Cávado valleys is floral and citrus-scented; Avesso from Baião is rounder and richer; Arinto gives backbone. Reds from Vinhão, almost black and high in acid, are a regional cult. The region also makes good traditional-method sparkling wines and aguardente.
appellations.terroir: Granite soils and Atlantic rainfall; the closer to the sea, the lighter and more acidic the wines. Inland, behind the Peneda, Gerês and Marão mountains, summers are hotter and drier.
appellations.nerd_note: The spritz in cheap Vinho Verde is now mostly injected CO2; the original prickle came from malolactic fermentation finishing in bottle, which is why old-school bottles were slightly cloudy.

appellations.name: Monção e Melgaço
appellations.grapes: Alvarinho, Trajadura; Pedral, Alvarelhão, Borraçal, Vinhão
appellations.summary: The northernmost subregion, along the south bank of the Minho river facing Galicia's Rías Baixas, and the home of Alvarinho (Albariño across the river). Protected from Atlantic rain by the mountains to the west and north, it is warmer and drier in summer than the rest of Vinho Verde, so Alvarinho ripens to 12.5 to 13.5% while keeping its acidity. Palácio da Brejoeira made the first prestige bottling here in 1976; Soalheiro, Anselmo Mendes and the Monção cooperative made the name international. Until 2021 only wines from here could be labelled Vinho Verde Alvarinho.
appellations.terroir: Granite with alluvial terraces near the river; a semi-continental pocket within the Atlantic north-west. Melgaço's higher, cooler vineyards (Soalheiro) give tauter wines than Monção's warmer valley floor.
appellations.nerd_note: Wines from here may be labelled with the subregion name alone, Monção e Melgaço, without saying Alvarinho.

appellations.name: Lima
appellations.grapes: Loureiro, Arinto, Trajadura; Vinhão, Borraçal
