appellations.summary: The valley of the Lima river around Ponte de Lima and Arcos de Valdevez, the homeland of Loureiro. Loureiro here is floral and citrus-bright, with laurel (louro), lime blossom and real tension. Quinta do Ameal showed in the 1990s that Lima Loureiro could age.
appellations.terroir: Granite, an open Atlantic valley with high rainfall and mild temperatures.

appellations.name: Cávado
appellations.grapes: Loureiro, Arinto, Trajadura; Vinhão, Borraçal
appellations.summary: The Cávado valley around Barcelos and Braga, close to the coast: light, aromatic Loureiro- and Arinto-based whites and fresh reds.
appellations.terroir: Granite, maritime climate, high rainfall.

appellations.name: Ave
appellations.grapes: Loureiro, Arinto, Trajadura, Alvarinho; Vinhão
appellations.summary: The Ave valley around Guimarães, Famalicão and Vila Verde: classic blended whites of Loureiro, Arinto and Trajadura and some of the region's best sparkling bases.
appellations.terroir: Granite; Atlantic influence moderated by distance from the sea.

appellations.name: Basto
appellations.grapes: Azal, Arinto, Trajadura; Rabo de Anho, Espadeiro, Vinhão
appellations.summary: The inland Tâmega country around Cabeceiras, Celorico and Mondim de Basto, behind the Marão foothills. Hotter summers and colder winters give fuller reds and the zesty, apple-scented Azal whites.
appellations.terroir: Granite and some schist, more continental climate.

appellations.name: Sousa
appellations.grapes: Loureiro, Arinto, Trajadura, Avesso, Azal; Vinhão, Espadeiro
appellations.summary: The Sousa valley around Penafiel, Paredes, Lousada and Felgueiras, where Aveleda, the region's biggest family firm, has its estate.
appellations.terroir: Granite, intermediate climate.

appellations.name: Amarante
appellations.grapes: Avesso, Azal, Arinto; Amaral, Vinhão, Espadeiro
appellations.summary: Around Amarante on the Tâmega, warmer and drier than the coast: Azal and Avesso whites and some of the region's sturdiest reds.
appellations.terroir: Granite, sheltered by the Marão.

appellations.name: Baião
appellations.grapes: Avesso, Arinto, Azal; Amaral, Vinhão
appellations.summary: On the north bank of the Douro next to the Port region's western edge, Baião is the home of Avesso, a full, textured white that ripens well in the warmer, sunnier slopes. Quinta de Covela, revived since 2011, shows how good it can be.
appellations.terroir: Granite slopes facing the Douro; the warmest, driest Vinho Verde subregion, a transition to the Douro climate.

appellations.name: Paiva
appellations.grapes: Avesso, Arinto, Loureiro; Amaral, Vinhão
appellations.summary: South of the Douro around Castelo de Paiva and Cinfães, a smaller subregion of hillside vineyards; known for reds as well as Avesso-based whites.
appellations.terroir: Granite and schist, south bank of the Douro.

appellations.name: Minho
appellations.grapes: Vinho Verde varieties plus international grapes
appellations.summary: The regional wine (IGP) designation covering the Vinho Verde area, used for wines outside DOC rules, such as higher-alcohol or oak-aged Alvarinhos, international varieties or experimental styles.
appellations.terroir: As Vinho Verde.

appellations.name: Trás-os-Montes
appellations.grapes: Bastardo, Marufo, Tinta Roriz, Touriga Nacional, Trincadeira; Côdega do Larinho, Fernão Pires, Gouveio, Malvasia Fina, Síria, Viosinho
appellations.summary: A large, thinly planted DOC covering the high country north of the Douro and east of the Marão. Its best wines are field blends from old vineyards and fresh, spicy reds from Valpaços; whites from Côdega do Larinho and Síria can be bright and herbal. Production is dominated by cooperatives (Valpaços, Chaves) and a few estates such as Valle Pradinhos near Macedo de Cavaleiros, whose cool-climate reds and Riesling-inflected whites made the region's name in the 1990s.
appellations.terroir: Granite and schist plateaus at 350 to 700 m, continental climate.
appellations.nerd_note: Boticas' 'vinho dos mortos' (wine of the dead) is buried in bottles under the earth, a custom said to date from villagers hiding wine from Napoleon's troops in 1809.

appellations.name: Chaves
appellations.grapes: Bastardo, Tinta Roriz, Trincadeira; Côdega do Larinho, Fernão Pires
appellations.summary: The valley of the Tâmega around the spa town of Chaves near the Spanish border: light, fresh reds and palhetes from granite soils, historically an IPR in its own right.
appellations.terroir: Granite valley at 350 to 500 m, colder and wetter than the rest of the DOC.

appellations.name: Valpaços
appellations.grapes: Tinta Roriz, Trincadeira, Bastardo, Touriga Nacional; Síria, Gouveio
appellations.summary: The largest and most productive subregion, around the town of Valpaços and its cooperative; fuller, warmer reds from schist and granite.
appellations.terroir: Schist and granite at 400 to 600 m.

appellations.name: Planalto Mirandês
appellations.grapes: Bastardo, Tinta Roriz, Touriga Nacional, Marufo; Síria, Malvasia Fina
appellations.summary: The high plateau around Miranda do Douro and Mogadouro, above the Douro's international canyon, where Mirandese (Portugal's second official language) is spoken. Old field blends, often ungrafted or very old, are being rediscovered by small growers.
appellations.terroir: Granite plateau at 600 to 800 m; extreme continental climate.

appellations.name: Transmontano
appellations.grapes: Regional and international varieties
appellations.summary: The regional (IGP) designation for Trás-os-Montes, used for wines outside DOC rules.
appellations.terroir: As Trás-os-Montes.

appellations.name: Távora-Varosa
appellations.grapes: Malvasia Fina, Cerceal, Gouveio, Bical, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir; Touriga Nacional, Tinta Roriz
appellations.summary: The sparkling-wine DOC of Portugal's northern Beiras, on the high plateau between the Douro and Viseu. Altitude (500 to 800 m) gives slow-ripening grapes with sharp acidity, the raw material for traditional-method Espumante aged on lees. Murganheira's cellars, cut into the granite at Ucanha, hold millions of bottles; Raposeira near Lamego is the other historic house. Still whites from Malvasia Fina and Cerceal can be very fresh.
appellations.terroir: Granite soils, high altitude, cold winters and big diurnal swings.
appellations.nerd_note: Murganheira's founder dug the cellars straight into the blue granite of the hillside, giving a constant temperature for long lees ageing without air conditioning.

appellations.name: Terras de Cister
appellations.grapes: Regional and international varieties
appellations.summary: The regional (IGP) name for the Távora-Varosa area, named after the Cistercian monks who planted its first vineyards.
appellations.terroir: As Távora-Varosa.

appellations.name: Bairrada
appellations.grapes: Baga, Touriga Nacional, Alfrocheiro, Castelão, Tinta Roriz; Maria Gomes (Fernão Pires), Bical, Cercial, Arinto
appellations.summary:
Bairrada makes two very different things brilliantly. Its reds, from Baga on clay-limestone, are among Europe's most structured: high acidity and dense, grippy tannins that need ten or twenty years to unfold into notes of sour cherry, tobacco, tar and forest floor. Traditional producers fermented with stems and aged in large old casks; old Garrafeiras from the 1950s to 1990s are some of Portugal's great bargains. Its sparkling wines, from Maria Gomes, Bical, Arinto and Baga, are crisp and toasty, sold in every price band, and have been made here since the 1890s.

Because ripening Baga is risky in a wet Atlantic autumn, many producers blended it with Touriga Nacional or international grapes in the 1990s, while purists, led by Luís Pato, Filipa Pato and the Baga Friends, insisted on Baga alone. The Bairrada Clássico category rewards the traditional path.
appellations.terroir: Clay-limestone hills (Jurassic marls) for the great reds; sands for lighter wines and whites; maritime, rainy and cool.
appellations.nerd_note: Luís Pato's Vinha Pan, Vinha Barrosa and Quinta do Ribeirinho Pé Franco (ungrafted Baga on sand) are the closest Portugal has to Barolo crus; he left the DOC for years in protest at its rules and labels most wines Beira Atlântico.

appellations.name: Beira Atlântico
appellations.grapes: Regional and international varieties
appellations.summary: The regional (IGP) designation covering Bairrada and the coastal Beiras, used by many top producers (including Luís Pato) for wines outside DOC rules. Formerly part of the Beiras IGP.

appellations.name: Dão
appellations.grapes: Touriga Nacional, Alfrocheiro, Tinta Roriz, Jaen, Tinto Cão; Encruzado, Malvasia Fina, Bical, Cercial
appellations.summary:
If the Douro is Portugal's Rhône, the Dão is its Burgundy. Touriga Nacional, native here, shows a finer, more floral face than in the Douro, with violet, bergamot and red cherry, and is often blended with Alfrocheiro (bright, red-fruited), Jaen (the Mencía of Bierzo) and Tinta Roriz. The reds have fresh acidity and fine, granitic tannins, and the best age for decades: the old Garrafeiras of the 1960s from the Centro de Estudos de Nelas and cooperatives can still astonish.

The whites are the other revelation. Encruzado, almost unique to the Dão, takes barrel fermentation and lees ageing like Chardonnay, gaining a smoky, nutty, saline texture over ten years or more. Modern producers such as Álvaro Castro, Quinta dos Roques, Quinta dos Carvalhais, Casa de Mouraz, António Madeira and Textura are among Portugal's most admired.
appellations.terroir: Decomposed granite at 400 to 700 m in a basin surrounded by mountains; warm, dry summers, cold wet winters, wide day-night swings.
producers: Álvaro Castro (Quinta da Pellada, Quinta de Saes)
appellations.nerd_note: Jaen is the same grape as Mencía in Spain's Bierzo; pilgrims on the road to Santiago are often credited with carrying it, though in which direction is still argued.

appellations.name: Serra da Estrela
appellations.grapes: Touriga Nacional, Alfrocheiro, Jaen; Encruzado, Malvasia Fina
appellations.summary: The highest Dão subregion, on the western foothills of the Serra da Estrela around Seia and Gouveia; vineyards reach about 800 m, giving the freshest, most mineral wines. Álvaro Castro's Quinta da Pellada and Quinta de Saes are here.
appellations.terroir: Granite, high altitude, cold winters and cool nights.

appellations.name: Terras de Senhorim
appellations.grapes: Touriga Nacional, Alfrocheiro, Tinta Roriz; Encruzado
appellations.summary: Around Nelas and Carregal do Sal, the historic core of Dão research (the Centro de Estudos Vitivinícolas at Nelas) and home of Casa de Santar.
appellations.terroir: Granite plateau at about 400 to 500 m.

appellations.name: Terras de Azurara
appellations.grapes: Touriga Nacional, Jaen, Alfrocheiro; Encruzado
appellations.summary: The Mangualde area (Azurara was the medieval name), home of Sogrape's Quinta dos Carvalhais and Quinta dos Roques.
appellations.terroir: Granite, 400 to 550 m.

appellations.name: Silgueiros
appellations.grapes: Touriga Nacional, Jaen, Alfrocheiro; Encruzado
appellations.summary: South-west of Viseu along the Dão river; warm, well-exposed slopes and some of the region's riper reds. Quinta da Falorca is the best-known estate.
appellations.terroir: Granite slopes, slightly warmer than the plateau.

appellations.name: Castendo
appellations.grapes: Touriga Nacional, Tinta Roriz, Jaen; Malvasia Fina
appellations.summary: The north-east of the Dão around Penalva do Castelo (formerly Castendo), on the plateau toward the Beira Alta.
appellations.terroir: Granite, higher and more continental.

appellations.name: Besteiros
appellations.grapes: Touriga Nacional, Baga, Jaen; Encruzado, Bical
appellations.summary: Around Tondela on the western side, toward the Caramulo mountains: wetter and more Atlantic, with lighter, fresher wines. Casa de Mouraz farms organically here.
appellations.terroir: Granite with some schist, more rainfall.

appellations.name: Alva
appellations.grapes: Touriga Nacional, Alfrocheiro, Tinta Roriz; Encruzado
appellations.summary: The southern subregion along the Alva river around Oliveira do Hospital, sheltered by the Estrela and Açor ranges.
appellations.terroir: Granite and schist, river valleys.

appellations.name: Terras do Dão
appellations.grapes: Regional and international varieties
appellations.summary: The regional (IGP) designation for the Dão and Lafões area.

appellations.name: Lafões
appellations.grapes: Arinto, Cercial; Amaral, Jaen, Touriga Nacional
appellations.summary: A small, rainy hill region between the Dão and the Vinho Verde country, around São Pedro do Sul, Vouzela and Oliveira de Frades. Its wines are a transition between the two: light, high-acid whites from Arinto and Cercial and sharp reds from Amaral (Vinho Verde's Azal Tinto) and Jaen. Production is tiny and mostly local.
appellations.terroir: Granite valleys of the Vouga, Atlantic-influenced and wet.
appellations.nerd_note: Lafões is better known in Portugal for its veal (vitela de Lafões) than its wine.

appellations.name: Beira Interior
appellations.grapes: Síria, Fonte Cal, Arinto, Fernão Pires; Rufete, Tinta Roriz, Touriga Nacional, Marufo, Jaen
appellations.summary: A big, high, sparsely planted DOC along the Spanish frontier. Síria, the local name for Roupeiro, gives citrusy, floral whites with real cut at altitude; Fonte Cal is a local white rarity. Reds from Rufete, Touriga Nacional and Tinta Roriz are lighter and more perfumed than in the Douro next door. Pinhel has a long sparkling-wine tradition; Cova da Beira, between the Estrela and Gardunha ranges around Fundão and Covilhã, has the most dynamic estates.
appellations.terroir: Granite and schist, 300 to 750 m, continental climate.
appellations.nerd_note: Síria is the same grape as Roupeiro in the Alentejo and Códega in the Douro: one variety, three regional names.

appellations.name: Castelo Rodrigo
appellations.grapes: Rufete, Touriga Nacional, Tinta Roriz; Síria
appellations.summary: The northern subregion around Figueira de Castelo Rodrigo, bordering the Douro Superior and Spain; warm, schist-and-granite hills with a hill-top medieval village. Quinta do Cardo is the best-known estate.
appellations.terroir: Schist and granite, the warmest part of the Beira Interior.

appellations.name: Pinhel
appellations.grapes: Síria, Fonte Cal, Arinto; Rufete, Marufo
appellations.summary: Around the fortified town of Pinhel; known for whites and a long tradition of sparkling wine, with its cooperative as the main producer.
appellations.terroir: Granite plateau at 500 to 700 m.

appellations.name: Cova da Beira
appellations.grapes: Rufete, Tinta Roriz, Touriga Nacional, Trincadeira; Síria, Fonte Cal, Arinto
appellations.summary: The basin of the Zêzere between the Serra da Estrela and the Serra da Gardunha, around Belmonte, Covilhã and Fundão (famous for cherries). The largest and most dynamic subregion.
appellations.terroir: Granite and schist in a sheltered valley.

appellations.name: Terras da Beira
appellations.grapes: Regional and international varieties
appellations.summary: The regional (IGP) designation for the Beira Interior area.

appellations.name: Bucelas
appellations.grapes: Arinto (dominant), Sercial (Esgana Cão), Rabo de Ovelha
appellations.summary: A small valley 25 km north of Lisbon whose DOC is for white wine only, built on Arinto: a grape with lemon, green apple and lime-blossom aromas and a ramrod of acidity that lets the wine age for a decade. The Duke of Wellington took a liking to it during the Peninsular War, and in Regency London it was sold as 'Portuguese Hock' or 'Lisbon Hock', compared to the Rhine Rieslings of the day. By the 1980s almost all vineyards belonged to a single estate and the name had nearly vanished; Quinta da Romeira, Quinta da Murta and newcomers revived it from the 1990s. There is also a little traditional-method sparkling Bucelas.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and clay marls in the sheltered valley of the Trancão river, with Atlantic winds funnelling through.
appellations.nerd_note: Bucelas is a white-only DOC built on one grape: Arinto must dominate every blend, with Sercial (Esgana Cão) and Rabo de Ovelha in support.

appellations.name: Colares
appellations.grapes: Ramisco (red), Malvasia de Colares (white)
appellations.summary:
Colares is one of the strangest and most romantic wine places in Europe. On the Atlantic coast below Sintra, its DOC vines grow in deep beach sand (chão de areia) on their own roots, because phylloxera cannot survive in sand; when the louse destroyed Europe's vineyards in the late 19th century, Colares boomed. To plant, growers dig trenches several metres down through the sand until they reach clay, lay the cuttings in, and fill back. The vines sprawl along the ground, propped on small canes to keep the grapes off the hot sand, behind fences of woven cane that break the ocean wind.

The red, Ramisco, is ferociously tannic and acidic when young and needs decades; old Colares (Viúva Gomes or the Adega Regional bottlings from the 1930s to 1970s) turns into something like old Nebbiolo crossed with the sea: dried cherry, tea, mushroom, iodine. The white, Malvasia de Colares, is saline and fresh. Production has fallen from over a million litres a year around 1950 to a few tens of thousands, as holiday homes replaced vineyards, and only a handful of producers remain.
appellations.terroir: Deep Atlantic dune sand over clay (chão de areia) for DOC wines; a few vines on the clay (chão rijo) nearby must be grafted and do not qualify for the classic style. Fog, salt wind, cool summers.
appellations.nerd_note: The cooperative, Adega Regional de Colares, held a legal monopoly on vinifying Colares wine from 1931 until the 1990s; its cask hall, fitted with tropical-wood vats of uneven sizes, still holds the region's stocks.

appellations.name: Carcavelos
appellations.grapes: Galego Dourado, Ratinho, Arinto, Boal, Seara Nova; Castelão, Preto Martinho, Negra Mole
appellations.summary:
Carcavelos is a fortified wine from the coast between Lisbon and Cascais, made by stopping fermentation with grape spirit and then ageing the wine for years in wood: amber, off-dry to medium-sweet, with notes of dried apricot, almond and orange peel and a salty finish from the Atlantic. In the 18th century it was a celebrated export; the Marquis of Pombal owned a vineyard estate in Oeiras and pushed Carcavelos into the English market, and shipments are recorded as far as the courts of Europe.

Then the suburbs came. Phylloxera, war, economic crisis and above all urban sprawl along the Lisbon to Cascais railway reduced the vineyards to almost nothing by the late 20th century. Revival began in 1983, when the Oeiras municipality and the Ministry of Agriculture replanted 5 ha at the Marquis's former estate under the Villa Oeiras project; by October 2024 about 32 ha were growing Carcavelos, with more planned. It remains one of the smallest DOCs in Europe.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and clay, sea-facing slopes beside the Tejo estuary, warm and windy with salt air.
appellations.nerd_note: Villa Oeiras is a rare case of a city council running a winery: its cellar under the Marquis of Pombal's estate ages the wine, and the project's stated goal is eventually a 100-year-old Carcavelos.

appellations.name: Alenquer
appellations.grapes: Touriga Nacional, Tinta Roriz, Castelão, Syrah, Alicante Bouschet; Arinto, Fernão Pires, Vital
appellations.summary: The most prestigious of the Lisboa table-wine DOCs, in a valley sheltered from the ocean by the Serra de Montejunto, which makes it warmer and drier than the coast. Quinta do Monte d'Oiro (whose Syrah, from Hermitage cuttings, put the region on the map in the 1990s) and Quinta de Chocapalha lead a group of estates making supple, well-built reds and fresh whites.
appellations.terroir: Clay-limestone hills behind the Montejunto range, rain shadow, warm days.
appellations.nerd_note: Quinta do Monte d'Oiro's owner José Bento dos Santos planted Syrah cuttings sourced from Hermitage, and its Reserva is often cited as Portugal's best Syrah.

appellations.name: Arruda
appellations.grapes: Castelão, Tinta Roriz, Touriga Nacional; Arinto, Fernão Pires, Vital
appellations.summary: Around Arruda dos Vinhos ('Arruda of the wines'), just north of Lisbon. A historic source of rustic red for the capital, dominated by its cooperative; easy, fruity reds and whites. The lines of Torres Vedras, Wellington's defensive forts of 1810, cross the area.
appellations.terroir: Clay-limestone hills just inland from the Atlantic.
producers: Adega Cooperativa de Arruda dos Vinhos

appellations.name: Óbidos
appellations.grapes: Arinto, Fernão Pires, Vital, Seara Nova; Castelão, Touriga Nacional, Tinta Roriz
appellations.summary: Around the walled medieval town of Óbidos (and its cherry liqueur, ginjinha). Cool, Atlantic-exposed hills give fresh whites and the region's best traditional-method sparkling base wines.
appellations.terroir: Clay and limestone, strong Atlantic influence.

appellations.name: Torres Vedras
appellations.grapes: Arinto, Fernão Pires, Vital, Seara Nova; Castelão, Tinta Roriz, Touriga Nacional
appellations.summary: One of Portugal's largest wine-producing municipalities, long the source of light 'vinho de consumo' for Lisbon. Its DOC wines are fresh whites and light reds; the biggest producers are cooperatives and Casa Santos Lima's neighbouring estates. The town gave its name to Wellington's Lines of Torres Vedras, which stopped Masséna's invasion in 1810.
appellations.terroir: Clay-limestone, Atlantic winds and fog.

appellations.name: Lourinhã
appellations.grapes: Alicante Branco, Boal Espinho, Malvasia Rei, Tália; Cabinda, Marufo, Tinta Miúda
appellations.summary: Lourinhã is a demarcated region for grape brandy (aguardente vínica), one of only a handful of brandy appellations in Europe alongside Cognac, Armagnac and Jerez. Thin, very acidic base wines from the windy coast north of Lisbon are double-distilled and aged at least two years in oak; the best are aged far longer. Production is tiny, led by the local cooperative.
appellations.terroir: Coastal clay and sandstone, cool Atlantic winds that keep base wines low in alcohol and high in acid, ideal for distillation.
appellations.nerd_note: Because it covers brandy, not wine, Lourinhã does not appear in the EU register of wine PDOs; it is protected as a spirit drink geographical indication.

appellations.name: Encostas d’Aire
appellations.grapes: Baga, Castelão, Trincadeira, Touriga Nacional, Tinta Roriz; Arinto, Fernão Pires, Vital
appellations.summary: A large DOC on the limestone foothills of the Serra de Aire and Serra dos Candeeiros, around Leiria, Batalha, Alcobaça, Fátima and Ourém. It has two subregions, Alcobaça and Ourém; the latter is home to Medieval de Ourém, a traditional blend of white Fernão Pires with a little red Trincadeira, fermented separately and blended, now a recognised style within the DOC. The Cistercian abbey of Alcobaça, whose monks planted vines here from the 12th century, has a wine museum.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and clay, karst hills, Atlantic-influenced to the west and warmer inland toward the Tejo.
appellations.nerd_note: Medieval de Ourém revives a style mentioned in medieval charters: about 80% white must and 20% red, fermented apart and blended in spring.

appellations.name: Lisboa
appellations.grapes: Regional and international varieties
appellations.summary: The regional (IGP) designation for the Lisboa region, called Estremadura until 2008, used by much of the region's production including many of its best-known estates.

appellations.name: DoTejo
appellations.grapes: Fernão Pires, Arinto, Talia; Castelão, Trincadeira, Touriga Nacional, Tinta Roriz, Alicante Bouschet
appellations.summary: A big DOC along the Tagus valley. Its signature white is Fernão Pires: aromatic, citrus-and-flower scented, sometimes barrel-fermented or late-harvested. Reds range from light, fruity Castelão from the floodplain to dense Touriga and Alicante blends from the sandy charneca. Most of the region's wine is sold as IGP Tejo; the DOC is used for more traditional, regionally typical wines.
appellations.terroir: Alluvial floodplain, sandy heath and clay-limestone hills; Mediterranean climate with Atlantic influence up the river.
appellations.nerd_note: The EU register writes the name as one word, DoTejo, a contraction of 'do Tejo' (of the Tagus), so the label does not read as plain 'Tejo', which is the IGP.

appellations.name: Tejo
appellations.grapes: Regional and international varieties
appellations.summary: The regional (IGP) designation for the Tagus valley, called Ribatejano until 2009; it covers most of the region's production.

appellations.name: Setúbal
appellations.grapes: Moscatel de Setúbal (Muscat of Alexandria); Moscatel Roxo; Antão Vaz, Arinto, Fernão Pires, Malvasia Fina and others in minor shares
appellations.summary:
Moscatel de Setúbal is one of the world's great fortified Muscats. Muscat of Alexandria grapes are fermented briefly, fortified with grape spirit to stop the fermentation, and then left to macerate on their skins for months (often five or six), so the wine draws out apricot, orange blossom, honey and spice (at least three months, often longer). It then ages at least 18 months in wood, where it turns from gold to amber and, after decades, to a deep mahogany with notes of dried figs, coffee and burnt orange, always balanced by fresh acidity. To be labelled Moscatel de Setúbal the wine must contain at least 85% Moscatel; blends with less are simply Setúbal.

Moscatel Roxo, a rare pink-skinned Muscat mutation that nearly disappeared in the 20th century, was saved largely by José Maria da Fonseca and makes a more intense, spicy wine. Most are sold at two to five years old; a small share is released at 10 or 20 years or more, and single-vintage bottlings from José Maria da Fonseca's 19th- and 20th-century stocks are among Portugal's rarest wines.
appellations.terroir: Limestone and clay slopes of the Serra da Arrábida around Azeitão and Palmela, warm and sheltered; also sandy plains inland.
appellations.nerd_note: The long skin contact after fortification is what sets Setúbal apart from most other fortified Muscats: the alcohol extracts aroma compounds from the skins for months.

appellations.name: Palmela
appellations.grapes: Castelão (dominant in reds), Alicante Bouschet, Touriga Nacional, Aragonez, Syrah; Fernão Pires, Arinto, Moscatel
appellations.summary: Palmela is Castelão's home appellation, on the same ground as the Setúbal DOC but for table wines (and a fortified Moscatel too). On the sandy plain, Castelão gives soft, juicy reds with red cherry and a touch of spice; on the limestone of the Arrábida it is firmer. The castle of Palmela, a former seat of the Order of Santiago, looks over the vineyards.
appellations.terroir: Sands of the plain and limestone of the Arrábida hills.
appellations.nerd_note: Periquita, the José Maria da Fonseca red launched in the 1850s, was so successful that Periquita became a synonym for the Castelão grape across Portugal.

appellations.name: Península de Setúbal
appellations.grapes: Regional and international varieties
appellations.summary: The regional (IGP) designation for the Setúbal Peninsula, used for most of its table wine.

appellations.name: Alentejo
appellations.created: DOC unifying eight subregions; EU registration 1996
appellations.grapes: Aragonez, Trincadeira, Alicante Bouschet, Castelão, Touriga Nacional, Syrah; Antão Vaz, Roupeiro, Arinto, Fernão Pires
appellations.summary:
The DOC covers eight scattered subregions rather than the whole Alentejo. The classic Alentejo red is a blend of Aragonez, Trincadeira and Alicante Bouschet: dark, plush, warm and spicy, with soft tannins, the style that made the region Portugal's bestseller in supermarkets and restaurants. At the top end, estates such as Mouchão (with Alicante Bouschet since the early 20th century), Esporão, Cartuxa (Pêra-Manca) and the Portalegre growers make wines of structure and longevity. Whites from Antão Vaz (tropical and broad) and Arinto (fresh) have improved enormously.

Vinho de Talha is the Alentejo's living Roman heritage: grapes are crushed into large clay jars (talhas), sometimes 1,000 to 2,000 litres, lined with a resin called pez, and fermented with the skins, which sink as the wine clears. By tradition the talhas are opened on St Martin's Day, 11 November. The style was formally recognised in 2010; in 2021, 23 producers made about 180,000 litres, a tiny but fast-growing niche.
appellations.terroir: Hot, dry plains and low hills on schist, granite, marble and clay; the Serra de São Mamede is the cool exception.
producers: José de Sousa (José Maria da Fonseca)
appellations.nerd_note: Pêra-Manca, Cartuxa's flagship red, made only in exceptional years, takes its name from a 'wobbly stone' (pedra manca) and is said to have been among the wines Pedro Álvares Cabral took to Brazil in 1500.

appellations.name: Portalegre
appellations.grapes: Trincadeira, Aragonez, Grand Noir, Alicante Bouschet, old field blends; Arinto, Roupeiro, Fernão Pires
appellations.summary: The northernmost and coolest subregion, on the granite and schist slopes of the Serra de São Mamede near the Spanish border, with vineyards up to 700 m and old field blends. It is the darling of the 'new Alentejo': fresher, lighter, more mineral wines. Symington bought Quinta da Fonte Souto here in 2017; Susana Esteban, Tapada do Chaves and Rui Reguinga are other names.
appellations.terroir: Granite and schist, altitude 400 to 700 m, higher rainfall than the plains.

appellations.name: Borba
appellations.grapes: Aragonez, Trincadeira, Alicante Bouschet, Castelão; Roupeiro, Arinto
appellations.summary: Between Estremoz and Vila Viçosa in the 'marble triangle', where the soils are pale limestone and schist over marble. The Adega de Borba cooperative (1955) was one of the first to bottle quality Alentejo wine; Quinta do Mouro near Estremoz is the subregion's star estate.
appellations.terroir: Marble-derived limestone and schist; slightly cooler and higher than the southern plains.

appellations.name: Redondo
appellations.grapes: Aragonez, Trincadeira, Alicante Bouschet, Castelão; Roupeiro, Fernão Pires
appellations.summary: South of Borba at the foot of the Serra d'Ossa, a subregion of warm granite and schist. Known for its cooperative and its tradition of pottery.
appellations.terroir: Granite and schist sheltered by the Serra d'Ossa.

appellations.name: Reguengos
appellations.grapes: Aragonez, Trincadeira, Alicante Bouschet, Moreto; Roupeiro, Antão Vaz
appellations.summary: Around Reguengos de Monsaraz, the largest subregion by production, home of Herdade do Esporão and the cooperative CARMIM. Hot, dry and schistous, it makes powerful, ripe reds. Monsaraz's hilltop village looks over the vineyards and the Alqueva lake.
appellations.terroir: Schist and some granite, very hot summers.

appellations.name: Vidigueira
appellations.grapes: Antão Vaz, Roupeiro, Perrum, Manteúdo; Alicante Bouschet, Trincadeira, Tinta Grossa
appellations.summary: Below the Vidigueira fault scarp, a 50 km escarpment that channels cooling Atlantic air over the vineyards, so this southerly subregion makes the Alentejo's best whites, especially from Antão Vaz. It is also the heartland of talha wine, around Vila de Frades and Cuba, where taverns still serve wine straight from the jar in November.
appellations.terroir: Schist and granite at the foot of the fault scarp, with Atlantic breezes.
producers: Adega Cooperativa de Vidigueira, Cuba e Alvito

appellations.name: Évora
appellations.grapes: Aragonez, Trincadeira, Alicante Bouschet, Touriga Nacional; Roupeiro, Arinto, Antão Vaz
appellations.summary: Around the UNESCO-listed city of Évora, home of the Fundação Eugénio de Almeida (Cartuxa, Pêra-Manca) and of Tapada de Coelheiros (Arraiolos). Granite and schist plains.
appellations.terroir: Granite and schist, rolling plain.

appellations.name: Granja-Amareleja
appellations.grapes: Moreto, Trincadeira, Aragonez; Roupeiro, Rabo de Ovelha, Manteúdo
appellations.summary: The hottest, driest corner of the Alentejo, on the Spanish border around Mourão and Amareleja, with poor schist soils. Old bush vines of the local red Moreto survive here.
appellations.terroir: Thin schist, extreme heat (Amareleja often records Portugal's highest temperatures).

appellations.name: Moura
appellations.grapes: Alfrocheiro, Castelão, Moreto, Trincadeira; Antão Vaz, Fernão Pires, Rabo de Ovelha
appellations.summary: East of the Guadiana around Moura, a town better known for olive oil; clay and limestone soils that hold water through the summer give fuller wines.
appellations.terroir: Clay-limestone, hot and dry.

appellations.name: Alentejano
appellations.grapes: Regional and international varieties
appellations.summary: The regional (IGP) designation covering the whole Alentejo, used for most of its wine, including many top bottlings that use varieties or blends outside DOC rules.

appellations.name: Lagos
appellations.grapes: Negra Mole, Castelão, Touriga Nacional, Syrah; Arinto, Síria, Malvasia Fina
appellations.summary: The westernmost Algarve DOC, from Lagos out to Sagres and up the Atlantic coast to Aljezur. Windswept and cooler, with a handful of small estates making fresh reds and whites.
appellations.terroir: Sandy and limestone soils exposed to Atlantic winds.

appellations.name: Portimão
appellations.grapes: Negra Mole, Castelão, Trincadeira, Touriga Nacional; Arinto, Síria
appellations.summary: The smallest Algarve DOC, around Portimão, Alvor and Mexilhoeira Grande; very little wine is bottled under the name.
appellations.terroir: Coastal sands and clays.

appellations.name: Lagoa
appellations.grapes: Negra Mole, Castelão, Trincadeira, Touriga Nacional, Syrah; Arinto, Síria, Malvasia Fina, Manteúdo
appellations.summary: The Algarve's most important DOC, stretching from Lagoa and Silves east to Albufeira and Loulé. The Lagoa cooperative (founded 1945) dominated for decades; estates such as Quinta dos Vales, Morgado do Quintão (with century-old Negra Mole vines) and Adega do Cantor have raised the bar, including the region's characteristic pale, savoury Negra Mole reds and an old tradition of dry fortified wine.
appellations.terroir: Red clay and limestone barrocal behind the coast, sheltered by the Serra de Monchique.
appellations.nerd_note: Negra Mole is so pale that its reds are often mistaken for rosés; the Algarve sold them as the local 'clarete'.

appellations.name: Tavira
appellations.grapes: Negra Mole, Castelão, Trincadeira; Síria, Arinto, Diagalves, Moscatel Graúdo
appellations.summary: The eastern Algarve DOC around Tavira, Faro, Olhão and Castro Marim toward the Spanish border; a few small producers and a fading cooperative tradition.
appellations.terroir: Limestone barrocal hills and coastal plain; the hottest, driest part of the Algarve.

appellations.name: Algarve
appellations.grapes: Regional and international varieties
appellations.summary: The regional (IGP) designation for the Algarve, under which most of its quality estates bottle their wines.

appellations.name: Pico
appellations.grapes: Verdelho, Arinto dos Açores, Terrantez do Pico, Boal, Sercial, Fernão Pires, Generosa, Galego Dourado, Malvasia
appellations.summary:
Pico is a single, near-perfect volcanic cone rising 2,351 m from the Atlantic, and its vineyards sit on the lava flows at its foot, below 100 m, on the west coast around Madalena, Criação Velha and Bandeiras and on the north coast at Santa Luzia. Settlers broke the black basalt into thousands of small rectangular pens (currais), each a few metres across, walled with loose stones to shelter vines from wind and salt spray; the vines root into cracks in the lava. The resulting grid, stretching for kilometres, is one of the world's great agricultural landscapes.

Historically Pico made a fortified Verdelho (licoroso), and the 2014 EU specification still defines DOC Pico around that style. Today the excitement is the dry whites, especially Arinto dos Açores and Terrantez do Pico: piercing acidity, flinty smoke, citrus and an unmistakable sea-salt finish. The Azores Wine Company, the Pico cooperative, Fita Preta and Insula are the leading producers.
appellations.terroir: Fresh basalt lava (lajido) with almost no soil; walls of black stone that also radiate heat at night; extreme exposure to wind and salt; maritime, humid climate with high disease pressure.
producers: Cooperativa Vitivinícola da Ilha do Pico (Picowines)
appellations.nerd_note: The currais walls, piled from stones cleared from the lava, were so extensive that, it is often said, their total length would circle the Earth twice.

appellations.name: Biscoitos
appellations.grapes: Verdelho, Arinto, Terrantez, Boal
appellations.summary: A tiny DOC on the north coast of Terceira island, named after the 'biscuit'-like jagged lava rock on which the vines grow in walled curraletas. It is known for fortified Verdelho, traditionally made by the Brum family's Casa Agrícola, whose museum documents the island's wine history; dry whites are increasing.
appellations.terroir: Rough, porous basalt lava fields beside the sea, sheltered by stone walls.
producers: Casa Agrícola Brum (Museu do Vinho dos Biscoitos)

appellations.name: Graciosa
appellations.grapes: Verdelho, Arinto, Boal, Fernão Pires, Terrantez
appellations.summary: The DOC of Graciosa, the flattest and driest of the Azores, a UNESCO biosphere reserve. Its dry whites, made mainly by the island cooperative, are fresh and saline; since 2019 the regional rules allow still, sparkling and fortified whites under all three Azores DOCs, Graciosa, Pico and Biscoitos.
appellations.terroir: Volcanic soils on a low, windy island.

appellations.name: Açores
appellations.grapes: Regional and international varieties
appellations.summary: The regional (IGP) designation for the Azores archipelago, used for most of the islands' modern dry whites, reds and rosés.

sites.name: Adega Cooperativa de Chã (Chã wines)
sites.text: The cooperative of about 85 Chã das Caldeiras growers makes the Chã white, red and rosé, the oldest Cape Verdean wine brand, at roughly 100,000 litres a year. Its first winery was swallowed by the 2014 lava flow; the growers refused to move to the coast and rebuilt inside the crater in 2015.

sites.name: Pico do Fogo
sites.text: Cape Verde's highest point and an active volcano whose 2014 to 2015 eruption overran the crater villages. Its vineyards climb the cone's lower flanks; the Pico do Fogo name is also used for a Maria Chaves reserva.

sites.name: Chã das Caldeiras
sites.text: The flat floor of the Fogo caldera, about 9 km across, is where nearly all Cape Verdean grapes are grown: bush vines in black ash between lava tongues, with the cone of Pico do Fogo on one side and the 1,000 m wall of the Bordeira on the other.

sites.name: Taylor's Port Lodge
sites.text: Taylor's lodge on Rua do Choupelo has aged Port since the house's earliest days; the company traces itself to Job Bearsley in 1692 and took its present name, Taylor, Fladgate & Yeatman, in 1838. Taylor's made the first single-quinta Vintage Port (Vargellas 1958) and the first commercial Late Bottled Vintage (1965). The lodge's cellars hold great vats and thousands of casks of tawny.

sites.name: The Yeatman
sites.class: Wine hotel of the Fladgate Partnership (2010)
sites.text: The Fladgate Partnership's wine hotel above the lodges, opened in 2010, with a cellar of Portuguese wine and decanter-shaped pool; part of the company's push to turn Gaia into a wine-tourism destination, followed in 2020 by World of Wine.

sites.name: World of Wine (WOW)
sites.text: A cluster of museums, restaurants and a wine school built by the Fladgate Partnership in restored lodges, opened in 2020. Its wine museum explains Portuguese regions and Port's history; it is the most ambitious attempt yet to explain Port to people who have never tasted it.

sites.name: Fonseca Port Lodge
sites.text: Fonseca Guimaraens, a house of Portuguese and Brazilian origins run for generations by the Guimaraens family, joined the Taylor's group in 1948. Its Vintage Ports, rich and opulent, come mainly from three quintas: Panascal in the Távora valley and Cruzeiro and Santo António in the Pinhão valley. Fonseca Bin 27 is one of the best-known reserve rubies.

sites.name: Croft Port Lodge
sites.text: Croft claims 1588 as its founding date, making it one of the oldest Port names; it has been part of the Fladgate Partnership since 2001. Croft launched Croft Pink in 2008, the first rosé Port, and its Vintage Ports come from Quinta da Roêda beside Pinhão.

sites.name: Graham's Port Lodge
sites.text: W. & J. Graham started as Glasgow textile merchants who, the story goes, accepted a debt paid in Port in 1820. The lodge, built in 1890 high on the Gaia hillside, is the Symington family's flagship visitor centre and holds the Vinum restaurant. Graham's is known for sweeter, fruit-rich Vintage Port from Quinta dos Malvedos.

sites.name: Cockburn's Lodge
sites.text: Robert Cockburn founded the house in 1815. Its lodge has one of Gaia's largest cask collections and a working cooperage; Cockburn's Special Reserve was for decades among the best-selling Ports in Britain. The Symington family took the brand over in 2010 and revived its Vintage Port, built around Quinta dos Canais in the Douro Superior.

sites.name: Dow's and Warre's (Symington, Travessa do Barão de Forrester)
sites.text: The Symingtons' Gaia base on the street named after Baron Forrester. Warre's, dating from 1670, is regarded as the first British Port company; Andrew James Symington, who arrived from Scotland in 1882, became a partner in 1905. Dow's grew out of Silva & Cosens (1798), which merged with Dow & Co in 1877; Symington became a partner in 1912. Dow's is the drier, firmer style; Warre's the most elegant and floral.

sites.name: Sandeman Lodge
sites.text: George Sandeman, a Scot, founded the firm in London in 1790. The silhouette of the Don, in Portuguese student cape and Spanish hat, designed by George Massiot Brown in 1928, became one of the first great drinks logos. Sandeman has belonged to Sogrape since 2002; the riverside lodge is one of the busiest visitor centres in Gaia.

sites.name: Caves Ferreira
sites.text: A. A. Ferreira, founded in 1751, is the great Portuguese-owned Port house, shaped by Dona Antónia Adelaide Ferreira (1811 to 1896), 'Ferreirinha', who bought and planted vast estates including Vesuvio and Vale Meão and became the most powerful figure in the Douro. Sogrape bought the company in 1987. Ferreira is known for tawnies and for the Casa Ferreirinha table wines, including Barca Velha.

sites.name: Ramos Pinto Lodge
sites.text: Adriano Ramos Pinto founded the house in 1880 and built a business in Brazil on daring Art Nouveau advertising posters, many displayed in the lodge's museum. Owned by Champagne Louis Roederer since 1990, Ramos Pinto pioneered research into Douro grape varieties and vinha ao alto planting, and its quintas include Bom Retiro and Ervamoira.

sites.name: Kopke
sites.text: Founded by Christiano Kopke, a German-born merchant, in 1638: the oldest Port name still trading. Kopke specialises in old Colheitas and white Ports, and was the first house to release 50 Year Old Ports when that category was created. Since 2025 its group (formerly Sogevinus, owned by the Escotet family) is called the Kopke Group, alongside Cálem, Burmester, Barros and Quinta de São Luiz.

sites.name: Cálem Lodge
sites.text: António Alves Cálem founded the house in 1859; its ships carried Port to Brazil and brought back tropical timber. The riverfront lodge, with fado evenings and a visitor museum, is one of the most visited in Gaia. Part of the Kopke Group.

sites.name: Burmester Lodge
sites.text: A house of English and German origins established in the 18th century, with a lodge right by the Luís I bridge. Burmester is particularly respected for old tawnies and Colheitas. Part of the Kopke Group.

sites.name: Offley Lodge
sites.text: William Offley's house dates from 1737; Joseph James Forrester, later Baron Forrester, made his name as a partner of Offley Forrester in the 19th century. Today Offley is part of Sogrape and its lodge sits on Rua do Choupelo.

sites.name: Niepoort
sites.text: A Dutch family house founded in 1842 and now run by the fifth generation, Dirk Niepoort, one of the Douro's most influential and restless winemakers. Niepoort is famous for Colheitas, rare Garrafeira Ports aged in glass demijohns, and for the Douro reds Redoma, Batuta and Charme from Quinta de Nápoles.

sites.name: Real Companhia Velha
sites.text: The direct descendant of the Companhia Geral da Agricultura das Vinhas do Alto Douro created by Pombal in 1756, privately owned by the Silva Reis family since the 20th century. It owns Quinta das Carvalhas opposite Pinhão and makes Port and Douro wines under several brands.

sites.name: Factory House
sites.text: The Georgian club house of the British Association in Porto, completed around 1790 to designs by consul John Whitehead. Its members, the British Port shippers, still lunch there every Wednesday, then move to an identical dining room next door to drink Port without the smell of food. The house holds a remarkable cellar of old Vintage Port.

sites.name: IVDP, Porto headquarters
sites.text: The Instituto dos Vinhos do Douro e do Porto, created in 2003 as successor to the Port Wine Institute of 1933, certifies every bottle of Port and Douro wine, runs the tasting chamber that approves Vintage and LBV samples, and each July its interprofessional council sets the beneficio. Its Porto building on Rua Ferreira Borges has a public tasting room.

sites.name: Cais de Gaia and the rabelo boats
sites.text: The Gaia quayside where rabelos, flat-bottomed boats with a square sail and a long steering oar, once unloaded pipes of new wine after a perilous trip down the rapids from the Douro. Railways, roads and dams ended the trade in the 20th century; restored rabelos with shippers' names now moor here and race each year on São João, 24 June.

sites.name: Museu do Douro
sites.text: The museum of the Douro wine region in Peso da Régua, housed partly in the 18th-century Casa da Companhia, the warehouse of Pombal's company. It holds the region's archives, and its researchers led the search that located 105 of the 335 original boundary stones.

sites.name: Casa do Douro
sites.text: Created in 1932 to represent the region's growers, the Casa do Douro kept the vineyard register (cadastro) and administered the points system until 2004. Its building in Régua is known for its stained-glass windows depicting the Port cycle. It was restored as a public association of growers in the 2010s and 2020s amid political dispute.

sites.name: Marcos pombalinos (Galafura group)
sites.text: Classified group of the granite boundary stones placed between 1758 and 1761 to mark the limits of the vineyards entitled to produce export-quality vinho de feitoria. 335 were set; the Museu do Douro has relocated 105. Many are inscribed FEITORIA with the year, a physical record of one of the world's first legal wine delimitations.

sites.name: Miradouro de São Leonardo de Galafura
sites.text: A granite outcrop at about 640 m with one of the great views of the terraced valley, celebrated in a poem by Miguel Torga, who called the Douro 'a geological poem'.

sites.name: Quinta do Vallado
sites.text: On the Corgo river just outside Régua, Vallado has belonged to descendants of Dona Antónia Ferreira for generations. Its dry reds and whites, a wine hotel with a contemporary schist-clad wing, and its role as a founding Douro Boy make it a symbol of the region's table-wine turn. It also farms Quinta do Orgal in the Douro Superior.

sites.name: Quinta da Pacheca
sites.class: Estate and wine hotel, Baixo Corgo
sites.text: A historic estate on the south bank opposite Régua, documented since the 18th century, now known for its wine hotel (including rooms inside giant wine barrels) and Port and Douro wines.

sites.name: Quinta da Gaivosa
sites.class: Alves de Sousa estate, Baixo Corgo
sites.text: The Alves de Sousa family's estate near Santa Marta de Penaguião, on cooler, higher Baixo Corgo slopes. Domingos Alves de Sousa was among the first growers to bottle Douro wines under his own name in the early 1990s; Gaivosa and Abandonado (from an old vineyard left almost wild) are its icons.

sites.name: Quinta do Côtto
sites.text: Owned by the Champalimaud family for centuries, at the western edge of the region near Mesão Frio. Its Grande Escolha, first made in the 1980s, was one of the earliest serious single-estate Douro reds.

sites.name: Mateus Palace
sites.text: The 18th-century baroque palace near Vila Real whose façade has appeared on every bottle of Mateus Rosé since 1942. The wine was never made here: Sogrape's founder paid the owners for the image (choosing a royalty-free lump sum, the story goes, rather than a fee per bottle). The house and gardens are open to visitors.

sites.name: Pinhão
sites.text: A small riverside village at the mouth of the Pinhão river, surrounded by famous quintas (Roêda, Bomfim, Foz, Carvalhas, La Rosa). Its railway station, reached by the Douro line in 1880, is decorated with azulejo panels of the vintage and the river. Most Vintage Port is grown within about 20 km of here.

sites.name: Quinta do Noval
sites.text: Above the Pinhão valley, Noval has been documented since 1715. Under Luiz Vasconcelos Porto in the 20th century it became famous for its 1931 Vintage, one of the most celebrated Ports ever made. AXA Millésimes has owned it since 1993, run by Christian Seely, and in 2019 it added neighbouring Quinta do Passadouro. After a 1981 fire destroyed its Gaia lodge, Noval moved its ageing to the Douro.

sites.name: Nacional vineyard (Quinta do Noval)
sites.text: A plot of about 2.5 ha within Noval planted with vines on their own roots (pé franco), never grafted onto American rootstock, hence nacional, 'national'. Phylloxera is present in the soil, so dying vines are replaced by layering. Yields are tiny; Nacional Vintage Port is made only in exceptional years and is the rarest and most expensive Port. The precise parcel location is not published; the point marks the quinta.

sites.name: Quinta do Passadouro
sites.text: Bought by Dieter Bohrmann in 1991 and by Quinta do Noval in 2019, adding 36 ha in the Pinhão and Roncão valleys; it had long supplied grapes for Noval's Vintage. The Passadouro brand was kept.

sites.name: Quinta do Cruzeiro
sites.text: On the eastern side of the Pinhão river near Vale de Mendiz, Cruzeiro was given feitoria status in 1761 and has supplied Fonseca since about 1870; its wines have been in the Fonseca Vintage blend since 1912. Fonseca bought it in 1973 and it was one of the first Douro properties replanted on wide patamares. It gives the dense black-fruit core of Fonseca's Vintage.

sites.name: Quinta de Santo António (Fonseca)
sites.text: About a kilometre north of Cruzeiro on a west-facing slope that falls to the Pinhão river, included in the first classification of 1757. It has supplied Fonseca's Vintage blend for about a century, bringing the exotic aromatics, and is farmed organically.

sites.name: Quinta da Cavadinha
sites.text: Warre's quinta in the Pinhão valley, in Symington hands since 1980. Its vineyards climb to around 500 m, and the altitude gives Cavadinha's single-quinta Vintage Ports a floral, fresh character that defines Warre's style.

sites.name: Quinta da Roêda
sites.text: Croft's home quinta, a broad amphitheatre of terraces immediately east of Pinhão, owned by Croft since 1889. It is the source of Croft's single-quinta Vintage and the backbone of its declared Vintage; visitors can tread grapes in its lagares at harvest.

sites.name: Quinta do Bomfim
sites.text: Dow's estate on the edge of Pinhão, bought by Silva & Cosens in 1896. It has a Symington winery and visitor centre and gives single-quinta Vintage Ports in non-declared years.

sites.name: Quinta da Foz
sites.class: Cálem's quinta at the mouth of the Pinhão
sites.text: Where the Pinhão meets the Douro, Foz has supplied Cálem since the late 19th century and gives its single-quinta Vintage.

sites.name: Quinta das Carvalhas
sites.text: A huge hill of terraces opposite Pinhão, rising to over 500 m, owned by Real Companhia Velha. Its round house at the summit looks over the whole Cima Corgo, and its old-vine blocks give some of the company's finest wines.

sites.name: Quinta de la Rosa
sites.text: Just downriver from Pinhão, La Rosa was given in 1906 as a christening present to Claire Feuerheerd, from a German Port family. Her granddaughter Sophia Bergqvist revived it as an independent estate in 1988, bottling its own Port and Douro wines when that became possible after 1986.

sites.name: Quinta do Junco
sites.text: A Taylor's property of about 46 ha of vines in the Pinhão valley, part of the core of its Vintage Port alongside Terra Feita.

sites.name: Quinta de Terra Feita
sites.text: Terra Feita, in the Pinhão valley near Quinta do Junco, has about 61 ha of south-facing vines and has been a mainstay of Taylor's Vintage Port for more than a century; in some years Taylor's releases it as a single-quinta Vintage.

sites.name: Quinta do Portal
sites.text: On the Sabrosa to Pinhão road at Celeirós, Portal built a reputation for Moscatel and Douro wines under the Mansilha family, with a barrel cellar designed by Álvaro Siza Vieira. The Fladgate Partnership bought it in 2024 (53 ha of vines, winery and 16-room hotel), its first Douro vineyards dedicated to table wine.

sites.name: Quinta do Infantado
sites.text: The Roseira family's estate at Chanceleiros near Covas do Douro, once owned by the Infante (a royal prince), hence the name. Infantado was among the first Douro farms to bottle and sell its own Port, from the late 1970s, and is known for less-sweet Vintage and LBV styles.

sites.name: Quinta Nova de Nossa Senhora do Carmo
sites.text: A historic north-bank estate near Covas do Douro, owned by the Amorim family (of cork fame), with a wine hotel and a notable range of Douro reds.

sites.name: Quinta do Crasto
sites.text: Perched on a ridge above the north bank between Régua and Pinhão, Crasto (from castrum, a Roman fort) belongs to the Roquette family. Its old field-blend vineyards Vinha Maria Teresa and Vinha da Ponte make two of the Douro's most sought-after reds; its infinity pool over the river is the region's most photographed view.

sites.name: Quinta do Seixo
sites.text: Sandeman's estate and visitor centre on the south bank opposite Pinhão, owned with the brand by Sogrape. The winery, with its robotic lagares, sits high above the river with a view toward Pinhão.

sites.name: Quinta do Bom Retiro
sites.text: Ramos Pinto's main estate in the Rio Torto valley, source of its single-quinta tawnies (10 Year Old Quinta da Ervamoira and 20 Year Old Quinta do Bom Retiro).

sites.name: Quinta Vale Dona Maria
sites.text: Cristiano van Zeller's estate in the Rio Torto valley, bought in 1996 with old field-blend vineyards; a founding Douro Boy. Van Zeller had earlier run Quinta do Noval for his family. Now owned by Aveleda.

sites.name: Quinta de Ventozelo
sites.text: One of the largest single estates in the Douro, on the south bank east of Pinhão, documented since the Middle Ages. Owned by Gran Cruz (La Martiniquaise group), it has been restored with a hotel and an interpretation centre on the estate's history.

sites.name: Quinta do Panascal
sites.text: In the Távora valley on the south bank, Panascal (acquired by Fonseca in 1978) produces Fonseca's single-quinta Vintage and was one of the first Douro quintas to open to visitors and to earn organic certification.

sites.name: Quinta de São Luiz
sites.text: A large estate at Adorigo on the south bank, the Douro home of the Kopke Group (Kopke, Cálem, Burmester), with a winery and stocks of old wines.

sites.name: Quinta do Tedo
sites.class: Estate at the mouth of the Tedo
sites.text: A French-owned estate where the Tedo river meets the Douro, making organic Port and Douro wines and running a guesthouse.

sites.name: Quinta de Nápoles
sites.text: Niepoort's winery in the Tedo valley, opened in 2007, built into the schist hillside. Here Dirk Niepoort makes Redoma, Batuta, Charme and an expanding range of fresh, lower-extraction Douro wines.

sites.name: Quinta de Roriz
sites.text: Roriz has been a celebrated vineyard since the 18th century and was among the first estates whose Port was sold under its own name; since 2009 it has been the vineyard base of Prats & Symington, the partnership between the Symingtons and Bordeaux's Bruno Prats that makes the dry red Chryseia.

sites.name: Quinta da Romaneira
sites.text: A grand north-bank estate between Pinhão and Tua, owned in the 2000s by a group led by Christian Seely and later converted into a luxury hotel.

sites.name: Quinta dos Malvedos
sites.text: Graham's principal estate, bought in 1890, on the north bank just upstream of the Tua confluence. Its broad south-facing terraces make Graham's single-quinta Vintage Port (Malvedos) and the heart of the declared Vintage blend.

sites.name: Quinta do Tua
sites.text: On the opposite bank of the Tua from Malvedos. The Ferreira family built its house in 1834; Cockburn's owned it from the late 19th century and its research vineyard, established by John Smithes, helped rescue Touriga Nacional from near-extinction. The Symingtons bought it in 2006 as a Graham's quinta (about 22 ha of vines).

sites.name: Miradouro de Casal de Loivos
sites.text: A balcony above Pinhão with a near-aerial view of the river's bend and the quintas of Bomfim, Roêda and La Rosa; the classic postcard of the Port vineyards.

sites.name: Alto Douro Wine Region (UNESCO)
sites.text: Inscribed by UNESCO in 2001 under criteria iii, iv and v: about 24,600 ha of terraced vineyards, villages, chapels and quintas, with a 225,400 ha buffer zone. The listing recognises roughly two thousand years of winemaking and two and a half centuries of regulation that shaped the landscape.

sites.name: Cachão da Valeira
sites.class: Gorge between Cima Corgo and Douro Superior
sites.text: A granite gorge whose rapids blocked navigation upstream until it was blasted open between 1780 and 1792, making the Douro Superior reachable by rabelo. Baron Forrester drowned here in 1861 when his boat capsized; Dona Antónia Ferreira, travelling with him, survived. Today a dam stills the water and the gorge marks the boundary of the Douro Superior.

sites.name: São Salvador do Mundo
sites.class: Chapels and viewpoint over the Valeira gorge
sites.text: A hill of pilgrimage chapels above the Cachão da Valeira, with a view over the Douro's most dramatic gorge and the first vineyards of the Douro Superior.

sites.name: Quinta de Vargellas
sites.text: Taylor's assembled Vargellas from three properties bought between 1893 and 1896 (one from a daughter of Dona Antónia Ferreira). It has its own railway halt from 1886, about 67 ha of vines plus the neighbouring São Xisto, and blocks of very old vines bottled in the best years as Vargellas Vinha Velha. Vargellas 1958 was the first single-quinta Vintage Port marketed as such, and the quinta's violet-scented wines are the backbone of Taylor's Vintage.

sites.name: Quinta dos Canais
sites.text: A vast estate on the north bank opposite Vargellas, the heart of Cockburn's Vintage Port; now farmed by the Symingtons, who took over Cockburn's vineyards and then the brand between 2006 and 2010.

sites.name: Quinta do Vesuvio
sites.text: Developed in the 19th century by the Ferreira family into one of the grandest estates in the Douro, with its own chapel, village and a long row of granite lagares. The Symingtons bought it in 1989 and make only single-quinta wines here, all still foot-trodden; with about 133 ha of vines it is the largest of the family's 26 quintas.

sites.name: Quinta da Senhora da Ribeira
sites.text: A south-bank estate across from Vesuvio that belonged to Silva & Cosens (Dow's) from 1890 to 1954; the Symingtons bought it back in 1998 and now release it as a Dow's single-quinta Vintage.

sites.name: Quinta do Vale Meão
sites.class: Birthplace of Barca Velha; Douro Boys estate
sites.text: The last great estate created by Dona Antónia Ferreira, planted from 1877 in a meander of the Douro near Pocinho. Ferreira's first Barca Velha (1952) came from here. Her descendants, the Olazabal family, began bottling under the Vale Meão name in 1999: a founding Douro Boy, with alluvial, granite and schist soils side by side in one bend of the river.

sites.name: Quinta de Ervamoira
sites.class: Ramos Pinto estate and museum, Côa valley
sites.text: Planted by Ramos Pinto from 1974 in the Côa valley with a large vinha ao alto vineyard. In the 1990s, construction of a dam that would have flooded it was abandoned after Palaeolithic rock engravings were found along the Côa; the quinta now has a museum, and the Côa rock art is a UNESCO site.

sites.name: Quinta da Leda
sites.class: Casa Ferreirinha estate, Barca Velha source
sites.text: Bought bare by Jorge Ferreira for Casa Ferreirinha in 1979 and planted from scratch near Almendra, toward Barca d'Alva. Since the 1980s it has been the main source of Barca Velha, with a winery built by Sogrape in 2001 and about 160 ha of vines dedicated to Douro DOC wine.

sites.name: Barca d'Alva
sites.text: The hamlet where the Douro leaves Spain and becomes wholly Portuguese, at the eastern end of the demarcated region. The railway arrived in 1887 and once continued to Salamanca; the section beyond Pocinho closed in 1988, and its reopening has been planned since the 2020s. River cruises end here.

sites.name: Pocinho
sites.class: End of the Douro railway line
sites.text: Today's terminus of the Linha do Douro, which runs along the river from Porto through Régua, Pinhão and Tua; the dam and lock here help make the Douro navigable for cruise boats.

sites.name: Adega Cooperativa de Favaios
sites.text: The cooperative of the plateau village of Favaios, whose Moscatel do Douro is so widely drunk in Portugal that 'um Favaios' is a bar order. Favaios sits at about 550 m, cool enough for Moscatel Galego to keep its freshness; the village is also known for its four-cornered bread.

sites.name: Blandy's Wine Lodge
sites.text: In the heart of Funchal, Blandy's lodge grew from properties John Blandy assembled from 1824 onwards, including parts of an old Franciscan convent. Its upper floors hold canteiro casks warmed by the sun under the roof; the tour shows the cooperage, the old wooden estufas and a library of vintages. Blandy arrived in 1808 and founded the firm in 1811; it is now the core of the Madeira Wine Company (Blandy's, Cossart Gordon, Miles, Leacock's).

sites.name: Pereira d'Oliveira
sites.text: A family firm founded in 1850 whose lodge on Rua dos Ferreiros holds one of the island's largest stocks of old Frasqueiras, sold only when the family judges them ready; bottles from the 19th century are still released and can be tasted in the shop.

sites.name: Vinhos Barbeito
sites.text: Founded by Mário Barbeito de Vasconcelos in 1946 and transformed by his grandson Ricardo Diogo Freitas from the 1990s, Barbeito makes the most precise, least caramelised Madeiras on the island, with no added colouring, and single-cask and single-grower releases. Its winery sits above Câmara de Lobos.

sites.name: Henriques & Henriques
sites.text: Founded in 1850, one of the few shippers to own significant vineyards. Its Câmara de Lobos winery makes estufa and canteiro wines from a wide range of ages; the firm is now controlled by La Martiniquaise.

sites.name: Justino's Madeira
sites.text: Founded in Funchal in 1870 as Justino Henriques and later renamed, Justino's is the largest Madeira shipper, with modern premises in the Cancela industrial area east of Funchal. Its Cruz brand is the biggest Madeira (and Port) brand in France, the island's largest market. Point approximate.

sites.name: Câmara de Lobos
sites.text: A fishing harbour west of Funchal, painted by Winston Churchill in 1950, surrounded by terraces of Tinta Negra and Malvasia climbing toward Cabo Girão. Câmara de Lobos and Estreito together grow a large share of the island's grapes.

sites.name: Estreito de Câmara de Lobos
sites.text: The hillside parish above Câmara de Lobos, with terraces up to about 600 m, is the island's single most important vineyard area and hosts the harvest festival every September. Sercial thrives in its upper reaches toward Jardim da Serra.

sites.name: Jardim da Serra
sites.text: The parish above Estreito, at 600 to 800 m, where cool, misty slopes give Sercial and some of the island's freshest wines.

sites.name: Cabo Girão
sites.text: One of Europe's highest sea cliffs, about 580 m. At its foot lie the fajãs, flat landslide terraces once reached only by boat or rope, where tiny vineyards are still worked, now accessed by cable car.

sites.name: Fajã dos Padres
sites.text: A strip of land at the foot of the cliffs west of Cabo Girão, cultivated by Jesuits from the 16th century. It is famous as the last refuge of Malvasia Cândida, the original Malmsey grape of Madeira, after oidium; a few rows still survive here, reached by a lift down the cliff.

sites.name: São Vicente
sites.text: On the wet north coast, São Vicente's terraces, sheltered by heather hedges, grow Sercial and Verdelho for both Madeira and the dry Madeirense whites. The cooler, greener north gives sharper, more saline wines than the south.

sites.name: Seixal
sites.text: A tiny north-coast village famous for its steep terraces of Sercial and Verdelho running down to black-sand beaches; it gives its name to some of the island's best table wines.

sites.name: Museu do Vinho e da Vinha, Arco de São Jorge
sites.text: A small museum on the north coast about traditional Madeira viticulture, with pergola training, harvest tools and old vine varieties.

sites.name: Porto Santo vineyards
sites.class: Dry neighbouring island, Caracol and Listrão
sites.text: Flat, arid and sandy, Porto Santo grows vines in low bushes protected by stone walls and reed fences. Its Caracol and Listrão grapes once supplied Madeira's shippers and are now being bottled again as distinctive salty whites. Columbus lived here after marrying a local governor's daughter.

sites.name: Palácio da Brejoeira
sites.text: A neoclassical palace built in the early 19th century near Monção. Its owner Maria Hermínia Paes began bottling Alvarinho from the estate's vineyards in 1976, and for years Brejoeira was the most expensive white wine in Portugal and the benchmark for Monção Alvarinho.

sites.name: Soalheiro
sites.text: In 1974 João António Cerdeira planted the first commercial vineyard of Alvarinho in Melgaço, at a site whose name means 'sunny place'. His children Luís and Maria João Cerdeira built Soalheiro into the best-known Alvarinho brand, with styles from barrel-fermented to skin-contact and sparkling.

sites.name: Anselmo Mendes
sites.text: Anselmo Mendes, nicknamed 'Mr Alvarinho', pioneered barrel fermentation, lees ageing and skin contact for Alvarinho; his Melgaço winery makes some of the most age-worthy Vinho Verde.

sites.name: Adega Cooperativa Regional de Monção
sites.text: Founded in 1958, the Monção cooperative made Alvarinho accessible with its Muralhas de Monção blend and remains the largest producer in the subregion.

sites.name: Quinta do Ameal
sites.text: Pedro Araújo's estate on the Lima, from the 1990s the proof that Loureiro could make serious, long-lived whites. Since 2019 it belongs to Esporão.

sites.name: Quinta de Covela
sites.text: A Renaissance-era estate overlooking the Douro at the very edge of the Vinho Verde region. Abandoned after financial trouble, it was revived in 2011 by Tony Smith and Marcelo Lima; its Avesso and Arinto whites are among the region's finest.

sites.name: Quinta da Aveleda
sites.text: The Guedes family estate since the 19th century, with romantic gardens and a goat tower. Aveleda's Casal Garcia (launched 1939) is one of the best-selling Vinho Verde brands worldwide; the group also owns Quinta Vale Dona Maria in the Douro and Quinta da Aguieira in Bairrada.

sites.name: Chaves (Aquae Flaviae)
sites.text: The Roman Aquae Flaviae, whose 1st-century bridge over the Tâmega still stands. The Chaves subregion around it makes light reds and palhetes, and the town gives its name to a smoked ham as famous as its wine.

sites.name: Valpaços
sites.class: Heart of the largest Trás-os-Montes subregion
sites.text: Market town of the Valpaços subregion, whose cooperative handles much of the region's wine; old field blends survive in the surrounding villages.

sites.name: Miranda do Douro
sites.text: A fortress town on the cliffs above the Douro's international canyon; the surrounding plateau is the Planalto Mirandês subregion.

sites.name: Boticas (vinho dos mortos)
sites.class: Buried wine tradition (IGP Transmontano, outside the DOC)
sites.text: In 1809, legend says, villagers buried their wine to hide it from Napoleon's invading army and found it improved when dug up. Boticas, in the Barroso highlands just outside the DOC boundary, still makes 'wine of the dead', aged in bottles buried in the ground.

sites.name: Caves da Murganheira
sites.text: Founded in 1947, Murganheira ages traditional-method sparkling wine in galleries hewn into granite near Ucanha; it also owns the historic Raposeira brand.

sites.name: Mosteiro de São João de Tarouca
sites.text: Founded in the 12th century, the first Cistercian house in Portugal; its monks planted vines across the Varosa and Barosa valleys, the origin of the Terras de Cister name. The monastery itself stands just south of the DOC's parish boundary.

sites.name: Mosteiro de Santa Maria de Salzedas
sites.text: A great Cistercian abbey of the 12th to 18th centuries in the Barosa valley, whose monks owned vineyards on both sides of the Douro.

sites.name: Ucanha fortified bridge
sites.class: Medieval toll tower over the Varosa
sites.text: A 15th-century fortified bridge with a toll tower, where the abbots of Salzedas collected dues on goods, wine included, crossing the Varosa.

sites.name: Palácio Hotel do Buçaco
sites.class: Neo-Manueline palace hotel with its own cellar
sites.text: Built as a royal hunting palace from 1888 inside the walled Buçaco forest and turned into a hotel in 1917. Its wines, made under the hotel's own label for about a century from Bairrada and Dão grapes, are aged for years and sold only in the hotel and its sister properties; bottles back to the 1940s remain on the list and are legendary for longevity.

sites.name: Caves São João
sites.text: Founded in 1920 by the Costa brothers at São João da Azenha, Caves São João built huge stocks of Bairrada and Dão reds (the Frei João and Porta dos Cavaleiros labels) and still releases old reserve wines from the 1960s onwards.

sites.name: Aliança Underground Museum
sites.text: The cellars of Caves Aliança (founded 1927), part of the Bacalhôa group, now host a museum of archaeology, minerals and ceramics alongside barrels and millions of bottles of sparkling wine.

sites.name: Caves Messias
sites.text: Founded in Mealhada in 1926, Messias is known for Bairrada Clássico reds and sparkling wine, and for its own Port business in Gaia.

sites.name: Luís Pato (Óis do Bairro)
sites.text: Luís Pato took over his family's vineyards in the 1980s and became Bairrada's best-known grower, making single-vineyard Baga (Vinha Pan, Vinha Barrosa) and an ungrafted Baga from sand. His daughter Filipa Pato makes 'authentic wines without make-up' nearby. The point marks Óis do Bairro, the family's home village; exact winery location not verified.

sites.name: Quinta das Bágeiras
sites.text: Mário Sérgio Alves Nuno's estate in the hamlet of Fogueira near Sangalhos: Baga fermented in open lagares with stems and aged in old casks, and long-aged bottle-fermented sparkling wines. A benchmark of classic Bairrada. Point at the hamlet.

sites.name: Mealhada (leitão and Espumante)
sites.text: The town on the old Lisbon to Porto road whose restaurants roast suckling pig (leitão à Bairrada) in wood ovens; the dish is always paired with Bairrada sparkling wine, whose acidity and bubbles cut the fat.

sites.name: Quinta dos Carvalhais
sites.text: Sogrape bought this estate near Mangualde in 1988 and built a modern winery, a key moment in the Dão's revival; its Encruzado and Touriga Nacional set modern benchmarks, and Duque de Viseu is one of Portugal's best-known red brands.

sites.name: Quinta dos Roques
sites.text: The Oliveira family's estate near Mangualde (with Quinta das Maias near Gouveia) became one of the stars of the 1990s Dão revival, with varietal Encruzado and Touriga Nacional. Point at the village of Abrunhosa do Mato.

sites.name: Quinta da Pellada (Álvaro Castro)
sites.text: Álvaro Castro's family estate at Pinhanços in the Serra da Estrela foothills, with old granite terraces and walled vineyards; with Quinta de Saes, it is the source of some of the Dão's most admired wines, including Primus (old-vine white) and the Pape blend. Point at Pinhanços.

sites.name: Casa de Santar
sites.text: A 17th-century manor in the village of Santar, one of the Dão's oldest wine estates, with a formal garden; now part of the Global Wines group. Santar's village of noble houses (Santar Vila Jardim) is a model of wine tourism.

sites.name: Paço dos Cunhas de Santar
sites.text: A 17th-century manor in Santar with a vineyard and restaurant run by the Dão Sul / Global Wines group.

sites.name: Quinta da Falorca
sites.text: A family estate in the Silgueiros subregion known for long-lived Touriga Nacional and Jaen, and the T-Nac label. Point at the Quinta da Falorca road stop.

sites.name: Adega Cooperativa de Pinhel
sites.text: The main producer of the Pinhel subregion, known for sparkling wine and Síria whites from high granite plateaux.

sites.name: Castelo Rodrigo
sites.text: A walled medieval village on a hill above the plains toward Spain, giving its name to the northern subregion of Beira Interior.

sites.name: Fundão and the Cova da Beira
sites.text: Fundão, famous for cherries, sits at the heart of the Cova da Beira subregion between the Gardunha and Estrela mountains, the most active part of the Beira Interior wine scene.

sites.name: Adega Regional de Colares
sites.text: The cooperative that held a legal monopoly on Colares wine from 1931 until the 1990s. Its long cask hall, lined with vats of Brazilian hardwoods of irregular sizes from 1931, holds the stocks of Ramisco and Malvasia, and old vintages are still sold.

sites.name: Adega Viúva Gomes
sites.text: A tiled 19th-century cellar in Almoçageme with the date 1808 over the door (the founding of the company). Viúva Gomes is the best-known name in old Colares, whose reds from the 1960s and earlier are prized for their mineral, tea-and-mushroom complexity.

sites.name: Colares sand vineyards (chão de areia)
sites.text: Low, sprawling Ramisco and Malvasia vines on their own roots in Atlantic dune sand, behind cane windbreaks, between Colares and the sea. Planting means digging through metres of sand to the clay below. The point marks the village; vineyards lie scattered toward Azenhas do Mar and Praia das Maçãs.

sites.name: Villa Oeiras (Marquês de Pombal estate)
sites.text: The Marquis of Pombal's former estate in Oeiras, whose vineyards supplied 18th-century Carcavelos. Since 1983 the municipality and the Ministry of Agriculture have replanted Carcavelos here and age it in the estate's old cellars, producing most of today's Carcavelos.

sites.name: Quinta do Barão
sites.text: An 18th-century quinta with manor, gardens and cellar at Carcavelos, one of the historic producers of the fortified wine before suburbs swallowed the vineyards; classified as a heritage site.

sites.name: Quinta da Romeira
sites.text: The historic Bucelas estate that for decades owned most of the DOC's vineyards; its Arinto whites (Morgado de Santa Catherina, Prova Régia) relaunched Bucelas in the 1990s. Point near the village.

sites.name: Quinta da Murta
sites.text: A small estate on the slopes of the Serra de Alrota making taut, saline Arinto and a sparkling Bucelas.

sites.name: Quinta de Chocapalha
sites.text: The Tavares da Silva family estate, with winemaker Sandra Tavares da Silva (also of Wine & Soul in the Douro): elegant Arinto, Touriga Nacional and Castelão, and one of the best Lisboa wineries.

sites.name: Quinta do Monte d'Oiro
sites.text: José Bento dos Santos's estate near Ventosa, Alenquer, where Syrah from Hermitage cuttings and Viognier made some of the most acclaimed Portuguese wines of the 2000s. Point at Monte d'Oiro locality.

sites.name: Mosteiro de Alcobaça and Museu do Vinho
sites.text: The great Cistercian abbey founded in 1153 (UNESCO), whose monks drained the valleys and planted vines and orchards. The nearby Museu do Vinho de Alcobaça, in an old wine warehouse, holds one of Portugal's largest collections on wine history.

sites.name: Quinta da Alorna
sites.text: A royal-era estate at Almeirim founded in 1723 and later owned by the Marquis of Alorna, one of the Tejo's best-known producers of Fernão Pires and Touriga blends.

sites.name: Casal Branco
sites.text: A large family estate (also a stud farm for Lusitano horses) near Almeirim, known for Falcoaria wines.

sites.name: Quinta da Lagoalva de Cima
sites.text: A 19th-century estate near Alpiarça owned by the Holstein Campilho family, known for whites from Fernão Pires, Arinto and Talia and for Lusitano horses.

sites.name: José Maria da Fonseca (Casa Museu)
sites.text: The family company's historic house and cellars in Vila Nogueira de Azeitão. Founded in 1834 by José Maria da Fonseca, a mathematician, it created Periquita (from the 1850s), Lancers rosé (1944, for the US market, in a crock-style bottle) and a library of Moscatel de Setúbal reaching back to the 19th century. Still run by the Soares Franco family.

sites.name: Palácio e Quinta da Bacalhôa
sites.text: A Renaissance palace and garden at Vila Fresca de Azeitão, with some of the oldest azulejo panels in Portugal. Its Quinta da Bacalhôa vineyard, planted with Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot in the 1970s by its then American owners, produced one of Portugal's first Bordeaux-style reds.

sites.name: Bacalhôa Vinhos (Azeitão winery)
sites.text: Bacalhôa's winery in Azeitão, combining Moscatel cellars with displays from the art and tile collections associated with its long-time controlling shareholder, José Berardo. Bacalhôa is one of Portugal's largest wine groups, with estates in the Alentejo, Bairrada (Aliança) and Douro.

sites.name: Casa Ermelinda Freitas
sites.text: A family estate on the Palmela sands run by Leonor Freitas since the 1990s; once a supplier of bulk wine, it became one of Portugal's most awarded producers, known for Castelão and Moscatel.

sites.name: Castelo de Palmela
sites.class: Castle of the Order of Santiago
sites.text: The hill-top castle that gives the Palmela DOC its name, seat of the Order of Santiago from the 15th century, with views over the vineyards of the plain and the Arrábida.

sites.name: Herdade do Mouchão
sites.text: The Reynolds family, of English origin, bought this cork estate near Casa Branca (Sousel) in the 19th century and planted Alicante Bouschet in the early 20th. Its traditional adega with granite lagares and old vats makes Mouchão and the rare Tonel 3-4, dark, powerful and long-lived reds, among the Alentejo's few historic icons.
